title: Pardes Rimmonim
text: The First Gate, called "Ten and not Nine":

It is known and well established that, in the matter of the number of the Sefirot, all who engage in this hidden wisdom have agreed unanimously that they are ten, and on this matter there is no dispute whatsoever.

Now this is one of the matters concerning which a covenant was sealed in the wisdom of the Sefirot. And we possess the Sefer Yetzirah, which is attributed to Abraham our father, peace be upon him; some attribute it to Rabbi Akiva, but this is not agreed upon.

Now the words of this book are deep and lofty, and they are hidden from the discerning eye of those who contemplate; and even though many varied commentaries have been written upon it, in all its parts we still require instruction. Yet we shall expound its words as far as is possible for our poor and limited intellect. These are its words: "Ten Sefirot of belimah: the number of ten digits, five opposite five, and the covenant of the Unique One set balanced in the middle, in the word of the tongue and in the word of the membrum (ma'or)." End of quote.

Although it occurred to us not to explain this Mishnah — for its depths and secrets are concealed from us, being certainly above our intellect, and no one can descend to the depth of its language except Rashbi, peace be upon him, and Rabbi Akiva, peace be upon him, whose stature flesh-and-blood does not attain — nevertheless, because of the obligation incumbent upon us, we shall expound it forcefully. And what there is to scrutinize in it: First, his statement "ten Sefirot of belimah, a number" — for in truth "a number" (mispar) is superfluous, since it would have been fitting to say "ten Sefirot of belimah corresponding to digits": why "a number"? Second, his statement "five" — what does he need it for? Third, according to his words they amount to eleven, for they are five opposite five, and the covenant which is in the middle makes eleven. Fourth, his saying "by the word of the tongue and by the word of the ma'or" makes it appear that there are two mediators (makhri'in), and why are there two? Fifth, what is his intent in explaining to us whether they correspond to the digits, for seemingly this is not relevant to the topic he is treating? Sixth, now that he has set out to explain [the Sefirot] by way of the bodily limbs, it would have been fitting for him to explain all the limbs in which the Sefirot are alluded to, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Soul, chapter 4, God willing. We shall say that the author of this book intended in this chapter to conceal the whole wisdom of the Sefirot and yet to establish it compellingly. He said that they are ten Sefirot; and because he said "ten" — from which some notion of limit and corporeality might follow, since they are divided by number — he said that they are "belimah," meaning two words, "beli mah," the intent being "without quiddity (essence)." For although we did not guard the utterance of our mouth in saying "ten," the true belief is that they are "beli mah," without quiddity. The intent is that they have no quiddity graspable by human beings, since they are unbounded and not apprehensible, being devoid of limit and corporeality; and that which is incorporeal can be apprehended only in the heart of the enlightened among the people of Israel, by way of vision, as in prophecy. The reason for the number ten, given that they are "beli mah," will be explained in the coming Gates, God willing. He said "a number of ten," etc., lest, out of the great difficulty posed by the limitation of our knowledge, we come to say that there exists nothing but the simple One; therefore he said that they are truly a number. And the term "Sefirot" is an expression of number (mispar), for number applies to them, even though they are "beli mah." The proof of this is their very name, that they are "Sefirot," an expression of number, as we have explained. And to establish that they are a number, and that their number is ten, he said "a number of ten digits." And the verse says (Psalms 8:4): "When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers."
Now from the verse it is established that the creation of the heavens and their hosts is by means of the "digits," which are an appellation for the Sefirot of the supreme King.

Now the digits are ten; thus it emerges that the Sefirot by which the world was created are ten — five against five. He found difficulty in that the verse says (Isaiah 48:13): "My hand also founded the earth, and My right hand spanned the heavens." Here it emerges that the heavens are the work of God's hand, which is five digits, and these are only five Sefirot and not ten. To this he said "five against five": since the heavens are the work of God's hand and the earth is the work of God's hand, it appears that certainly the two together are ten — and this is "five against five": five on the right and five on the left, the right for the making of the heavens and the left for the making of the earth. "And the singular covenant set in the middle." He found difficulty in that this is not compelling, for one might say that they are five, or that they are twenty. The reason is that the digits are twenty — ten on the hands and ten on the feet, totaling twenty — [and one might say the same of the Sefirot]. Should you say that the ten of the feet are a shadow and likeness of the ten of the hands, so that there are never more than ten Sefirot — the allusion being that the ten Sefirot of Beriah are a shadow and garment to the ten Sefirot of Atzilut, as we shall explain in the Gate of ABiYA, God willing — then by the same logic we might say that there are never more than five, the five on the left being a shadow to the five on the right, so that there are never more than five Sefirot; or the argument returns and we might say they are twenty. To this he establishes both at once by saying "and the singular covenant," etc. The sum of the matter is that, since between the five and the five we find a union and a covenant that unites them, the five on the right and the five on the left are one thing and one matter, whose total is ten Sefirot — which is not what we find between the ten on the hands and the ten on the feet, which appear to be two arrays, each of ten, one a shadow and garment to the other. And the mediator between the five and the five is the "tongue," which mediates between the digits of the hands, and the "covenant of the ma'or" mediates between the ten of the feet. And regarding the Sefirot in this matter — that they are five against five — the commentators gave two explanations. The first: that they arranged the Sefirot into two arrays. The first array is Keter, Chokhmah, Binah, Gedulah, Gevurah — these are five — and they said these are to govern the upper [worlds]. And Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, and Malkhut are the second array, to govern the lower [worlds]. And although their statement "to govern the upper" and "to govern the lower" is not agreed upon by us, in the matter of the division of the Sefirot they aimed correctly. For such is the view of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in several places, and especially regarding the tefillin: that the four passages of the head are Chokhmah and Binah, Gedulah, Gevurah; and in the arm they are Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod — thus they explained in the Zohar, Parashat Va'etchanan (folio 264a). And although these matters require vigorous study — for he wrote elsewhere that the four passages are the four letters [of the Name] — nevertheless we derive from the totality of his words that the Sefirot are divided into two arrays, as the commentators said. Likewise, regarding the chariots within the Sefirot, they explained in the Tikkunim (in the Introduction, folio 3, and in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, folio 111) that the "face of a man" upon the Throne is Chokhmah — "koach mah" (the power of "mah"), equal in numerical value to "Adam" — and the eagle is Binah, the lion is Chesed, and the ox is Gevurah; this is the upper chariot. And beneath it a second chariot: the "face of a man" is Tiferet; Netzach, Hod, Yesod are lion, ox, eagle — this is the second chariot. And the supernal Keter includes all above, and Malkhut includes all below. Thus he divided the Sefirot into two arrays, as mentioned. And besides these there are many further proofs, but we shall not elaborate, so as not to stray from our purpose.

Now according to this explanation we shall expound this Mishnah, namely that Tiferet is the "singular covenant" that ascends higher and higher in the secret of Da'at, binding the upper to the lower by its ascent into the first three Sefirot, its mediating among the "arms" (Chesed and Gevurah), and its emanating into the Netzachs [Netzach and Hod], Yesod, and Malkhut. Thus "the singular covenant, by the word of the tongue and by the word of the ma'or, is set in the middle" — meaning, in the middle of the upper ten digits, the mediator is Tiferet, which is called "the word of the tongue," as I shall explain. He said "the singular covenant," for a covenant (brit) involves cutting and severing, and through the cutting of that thing the bond of the covenant is made — this is the meaning of "brit." Some read "union" (yichud) and some read "singular" (yachid), and both amount to the same place. The preferable reading is "union" (yichud), for through the covenant comes the union, which is the bond of the matter, its strengthening, and its unification. Some wish to interpret "the word of the tongue" as referring to Binah, but according to our approach it is to be interpreted as Tiferet. Even though "the tongue" is an appellation for Binah and not for Tiferet, he did not say "the tongue" but "the word of the tongue" — which is the voice and speech that issues from the tongue, that is, by means of the tongue.

Now the voice is composed of water, fire, and air, as is well known, and these are the three aspects of Tiferet — for it is the air [spirit] that mediates between the water and the fire of Chesed and Gevurah.

Now he did not intend the bodily limb, the tongue, for from that it would be difficult, since then they would be eleven, counting the mediator. Rather, the mediator is the voice, which is Tiferet, in the secret of its ascent to Binah, which is the tongue — which is the shofar from which the voice issues, composed of water, fire, and air. And this is the aspect of Tiferet that ascends among the first three Sefirot, and mediates between Gedulah and Gevurah — which indicates the binding of the five upper to the five lower, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions, God willing. And "the word of the ma'or" is the covenant of circumcision (brit milah); and the meaning of "ma'or" is like "ke-ma'ar ish ve-loyot" (1 Kings 7:36), as the Sages explained (Yoma 54a): "ke-ma'ar," like the joining of a man with his consort (loyah), who is the female. And the intent is to the union which is between the ten digits of the feet, by means of the ma'or that unites them. This explanation is compelling: that "the word of the tongue" unites the ten digits of the hands, and "the word of the ma'or" unites the ten digits of the feet — from what they explained in chapter six [of Sefer Yetzirah], whose words are: "He sealed for him a covenant between the ten digits of his feet, which is the covenant of circumcision, and between the ten digits of his hands, which is the covenant of the tongue." End of quote.
Now this Mishnah has been explained according to the interpretation that the commentators gave concerning "five against five."

We shall further explain this Mishnah according to another interpretation that the commentators gave of "five against five," which is more fitting and acceptable, and is also agreed upon in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in many places. The matter is: five on the right and five on the left. The five on the right are five Sefirot whose inclination is mostly toward the side of Chesed, which is the right — namely Keter, Chokhmah, Gedulah, Netzach, Tiferet; and the five on the left are five Sefirot whose inclination is mostly toward the side of Din [judgment], which is the left — namely Binah, Gevurah, Hod, Yesod, Malkhut. And although Tiferet is essentially the middle line, its root is Chesed, as is known that it inclines toward Chesed, and its leaning is to the right. And Binah is related to Din in its aspect, for it is called "the worker of mighty deeds (gevurot)," since from it judgments are aroused, as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 6. Likewise Hod, of which it is said (Daniel 10:8): "and my splendor (hodi) was turned within me into corruption"; "all the day [I am] faint (davah)" (Lamentations 1:13) — the same letters as "Hod." Yesod, too, has its principal inclination toward the side of Gevurah. So too Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 13, folio 29b) concerning "the ninth, with joy," etc., whose words are: "And the Tzaddik [Yesod] takes from the left, and the central pillar [Tiferet] takes from the right."

And he further explained there (in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, folio 125, belonging to the aforementioned passage) regarding this very matter, whose words are: "The Tzaddik [Yesod] takes to the left, which is Isaac — 'ketz chai,' 'Chai Olamim' (Life of Worlds) — bound to the left," etc. And although the passage in its place requires broad explanation and fine study, from the totality of his words it emerges for us that Yesod's principal inclination is toward the left, the opposite of Tiferet. And it is possible that this is the reason for the two mediators, besides other reasons there are for the matter, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Mediators, chapter 4, God willing. Malkhut, too, is essentially Din, for it is well known by name among all the Kabbalists that it is called "the lenient attribute of judgment" (middat ha-din ha-rafah). And although in some places [sources] seemingly dispute this, these matters are well-founded foundations, like firmly planted nails, and the ruling is a true ruling.
Now these Sefirot, in their order, are two hands: the right hand is Keter, Chokhmah, Gedulah, Netzach, Tiferet; and the five on the left are the left hand: Binah, Gevurah, Hod, Yesod, Malkhut.

Now Tiferet is the "covenant of the tongue," which is the mediator between Din and the Chasadim, as is known, and it is itself among the count of the ten. Likewise the "covenant of the ma'or" — although its root is in Yesod — according to this also alludes to Tiferet, for "body and covenant we reckon as one," as is explained in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Tikkunim many times.
Now it emerges, according to this, that between [the] ten and [the] ten there is no mediation, as there is mediation between five and five, as explained above in chapter 1.
Now this Mishnah has been explained — a second interpretation — according to what the commentators explained regarding "five against five."

We shall further explain this Mishnah — a third interpretation, by another approach to "five against five" — according to what seems right to us; and let him who chooses, choose for himself. Namely, his saying "five against five" does not refer to the aforementioned digits; for he moved from the matter of the ten to explain to us the mediation between Din and Chesed, the order of the mediation, and the matter of those that require mediation. Therefore he said that they are "five against five": that Tiferet mediates between Chokhmah and Binah in the secret of Da'at, when it ascends to Keter, as we shall elaborate in the Gate of the Mediators, God willing. Thus [we have] two, one against one: Chokhmah against Binah, for this [Chokhmah] is the root of Chesed and this [Binah] is the root of Gevurah. Furthermore, Tiferet mediates between Gedulah and Gevurah, as is known; and Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 30, folio 75) on the verse "And there was evening and there was morning" as follows: "'And God called the firmament Heaven' — 'And God (Elohim) called' is the supernal Mother (Ima); 'the firmament Heaven' is the central pillar, which is between right and left and includes both; this is the meaning of 'and there was evening and there was morning' — and these are the 'evening' of Isaac and the 'morning' of Abraham." End of quote.

And although from the plain sense of the words of this passage there is a proof for our intent, nevertheless, since it has come to hand, let us say a small matter concerning it, and let it not depart without lodging [due attention]. There are points to scrutinize in it: First, his saying "And God called — this is the Mother": have we not heard before now that every [occurrence of] "Elohim" in the account of Creation alludes to Binah? Second, what is his intent in saying "Mother (Ima)" and not "Binah," which is its more well-known name? Third, his saying "the central pillar, which is between right and left" — since he said "the central pillar," did we not know that the intent is that it is in the middle of the right and the left, which are Gedulah and Gevurah, that he needed to elaborate, "which is," etc.? Fourth, now that he set out to explain "which is between right and left," let him say "Tiferet, which is," etc., and be silent about "the central pillar," which appears redundant. Fifth, his saying "which is between right and left and includes both" is redundant, for "includes both" is the same as "between right and left." Sixth, his saying "this is the meaning of 'and there was evening and there was morning'" — for seemingly there is no proof at all for his intent from the verse. We shall say that Rashbi, peace be upon him, found difficulty in the verse "And God called the firmament Heaven": for the firmament (raki'a) is Tiferet, and Heaven (shamayim) is also Tiferet — so what is the verse's intent in saying "And God called the firmament Heaven," which makes it appear that "firmament" and "Heaven" are not one thing? To this he answered, "Elohim — this is the supernal Mother." The explanation, as if to say: you already know that every "Elohim" in [the account of] Creation is in Binah, and this "Elohim" is in Binah by the aspect of its relation to the lower [beings] — that it is the one which emanates, that is, which brings forth the emanated [beings] — and from there it is called "Mother"; and this is what he said, "this is the supernal Mother." "The firmament Heaven — this is the [central] pillar," etc. The explanation: Tiferet has two modes of existence. The one is from the side of Chokhmah, and it is a more refined existence, in that it is the secret of the line of Rachamim [mercy], which is emanated from Keter and spread to Chokhmah, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Order of Emanation, God willing. And this is the mode of existence to which Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, is a chariot, as explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 13, folio 29a), whose words are: "And Jacob is certainly the form of the central pillar from the outer side. But was not Moses there too? Rather, [Moses] was from the inner side, and this [Jacob] from the outer side — this one from the body, and this one from the soul." End of quote.

Now this mode of existence — which is its aspect with respect to Rachamim, without the compounding of Chesed and Din with it — is called "soul" (nishmata) relative to the mode of existence that is newly produced from the blending and compounding; and this "soul" is called "firmament" (raki'a). And we may say, by way of letter-combination, "raka yod" (the yod was spread out), for it is the mode of existence that was spread out and extended from Keter by means of the yod, which is Chokhmah. And this mode of existence he indicated by his expression "the central pillar" — meaning the central pillar and line, which has no admixture of Chesed and Din at all, but is between the two; and this is what he said, "which is between right and left." And by means of Binah this firmament was rectified, and it was clothed in the totality of fire and water, which is called "Heaven" (shamayim) — and this is "He established the heavens through understanding (tevunah)" (Proverbs 3:19). And the aspect that encompasses this mode of existence is Binah, called "Mother" (Ima), which is the existence of the letter heh — which is three vavs, which are the three lines, Chesed, Din, and Rachamim — as we shall explain in the Gate of Existence, God willing. Therefore he said "and includes both" — meaning, from the side of the Mother it includes the right and the left, which is the garment that is clothed upon, and crowns, the more refined mode of existence. And there is a proof for this from the Zohar, Parashat Yitro (folio 84a), whose words are, on the verse "Go forth and gaze, O daughters of Zion, etc., upon the crown with which his mother crowned him" [Song of Songs 3:11]: "What is 'with the crown'? Rabbi Yitzchak said: as it is written, 'And Saul and his men were encircling (otrim) David' [1 Samuel 23:26] — because he is crowned with white, with red, with green, with all colors, all of which are included in it and encircle it. Rabbi Yehudah said: 'with the crown with which his mother crowned him' — what is the crown? As it is written, 'Israel, in whom I will be glorified (etpa'er)' [Isaiah 49:3], and it is written, 'and the house of My glory (tiferet) I will glorify (afa'er)' [Isaiah 60:7]." End of quote.

And he explained "King Solomon" [as] the King to whom the peace (shalom) belongs — that is, Tiferet — and Yesod, "peace is his." And the crown is the mode of existence called "Heaven" (shamayim), which surrounds his simple mode of existence called "firmament" (raki'a), emanated from Chokhmah. And this is "with the crown with which his mother crowned him," which is the "Elohim" mentioned in the matter before us. Therefore he said above, "this is the Mother," which is Binah, the mother of the children. And "atarah" (crown) is an expression of encircling and enveloping, as in "And Saul and his men were encircling David," that is, surrounding. And he explained that this crowning is in three colors: white, from the side of Chesed; red, from the side of Gevurah; and green, compounded of the two, which is the blend blended by the "man in between" (the mediator), Tiferet. And lest we err to say that the white and the red are not in the existence of Tiferet, but only the green, he said "all of them are included in it and encircle it." The explanation: "King Solomon," which is the spiritual aspect from the side of Chokhmah — also called "King Solomon," as I shall explain in [the Gate of] the Values of the Allusions, God willing — is surrounded by the three colors, and they truly encircle it. And it is white with respect to its aspect toward Chesed, red with respect to its aspect toward Gevurah, and green with respect to the aspect of both in the equilibrium of the blend; and all of them surround it and crown it. And Rabbi Yehudah explained "with the crown" in another way, adding to Rabbi Yitzchak and saying that it is not only this, but the crown is the totality of all six extremities (ketzavot) — for with respect to this aspect the appellation "Tiferet" is apt, since it is from the term "pe'orot" (boughs), and like "pa'arei ha-migba'ot" (the adornments of the caps) (Ezekiel 39:28), meaning branches — that is, that it branches out into six extremities, and the six extremities are its branches. And this is what is said: "Israel, in whom I will be glorified (etpa'er)." And the explanation: Binah says of Tiferet, which is called "Israel," that in it she glories and branches out into boughs.

And he further brought a proof from the verse "and the house of My glory I will glorify (afa'er)," for she branches out and glories in her boughs. And he means: the "house" of Tiferet above is Binah, for there too is its dwelling (Shekhinah), since it "reaches from end to end" [Exodus 26:28] — from the [one] end of the heavens, which is Binah, to the [other] end of the heavens, which is Malkhut. And just as Malkhut is a "house" for Tiferet, so too is Binah; and this is "the house of My glory I will glorify." The explanation: she branches out together with the boughs of Tiferet, which belong to its measure. Or he means that Malkhut is the "house" for Tiferet. And Binah says "the house of My glory," which is the glory (tiferet) from my side — for from the side of Binah, it [Tiferet] also includes the boughs for its house, which is Malkhut — "I will glorify and branch out," in the secret that she includes six boughs from its side, that it is clothed six within six; and this is "with the crown," which is this crowning and clothing. Thus far [the Zohar]. And this is what is intended in the verse "And God called," [referring to] the Mother who crowns the firmament with the crown called "Heaven." And he brought a proof for this from the verse "And there was evening and there was morning, one day," explaining "evening" as Isaac and "morning" as Abraham. In their totality together, Tiferet comes into being and is clothed — which is called "one day," and this is "Heaven." And the totality of "Heaven" (shamayim) is "day," which is fire and water (esh u-mayim), evening and morning. And therefore he said "one day" (yom echad) — unified, for it unifies the two aspects. And we may say that from there [come] the twelve hours, in that it is seen [as] vav in its full spelling, which equals "echad" (one). And the explanation: two faces unify [it]. A vav from the right side is one face, a vav from the left side is one face, and an alef in the middle unifies the two faces together. And this is "echad" (one); and the two vavs are the twelve hours: six [hours] of the rising of the morning until midday, which is Chesed; six from noon until night, which is the evening, Gevurah — this is "one day." There is no need to elaborate here. And it would have been possible to multiply proofs concerning the matter of Tiferet's mediation between Gedulah and Gevurah; but since it is a simple and agreed-upon matter, we needed this only in order to understand this passage properly. And we have derived that Tiferet mediates between Gedulah and Gevurah, and they are two, one against one.

Tiferet further mediates between Gedulah and Hod, and between Gevurah and Netzach. The reason is that Gedulah and Netzach are the right side, Chesed; and Gevurah and Hod are Din, the left; and they require mediation. And there is some proof for this from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Parashat Pinchas, folio 244a), whose words are: "And in the first composition: 'I have gathered my myrrh with my spice' [Song of Songs 5:1] — the right arm with the left thigh; 'my honeycomb with my honey' — Jacob with Rachel; 'my wine with my milk' — the left arm with the right thigh. Chesed with Hod — these are the right arm with the left thigh; Jacob with Rachel — the central pillar with Malkhut; Gevurah with Netzach — these are the left arm with the right thigh. And why are His attributes thus [crossed]? Rather, it is a secret that says thus. David said here, 'Let Your priests be clothed in righteousness, and let Your devoted ones sing for joy' [Psalms 132:9], and it is said there [that] 'and let Your Levites sing for joy' he ought to have said. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: it is not the way of the world to change My attributes; rather, after you have invited Me, it is for Me to do your will. From here we learn that a householder who invites even a king — the king must do the host's will; and therefore we have established: 'Whatever the master of the house tells you, do,' etc. And with all this, this secret is fitting," etc. End of quote.

What there is to be roused about in this passage is the prolixity of its language and the repetition of the matter, albeit not in different words. In his saying "the right arm with the left thigh, Chesed with Hod," etc. — have we not heard before now that the two arms are Gedulah (the right arm) and Gevurah (the left arm), and the two legs which are Netzach (the right leg) and Hod (the left leg)? And what need is there for this prolixity in explaining matters that are simple? Second, from the outset he should have used brief and clear language: "my myrrh with my spice" — Chesed with Hod; "my honeycomb with my honey" — the central pillar with Malkhut; "my wine with my milk" — Gevurah with Netzach; and been silent about "thighs and arms," so that he would not then need to explain them afterward. Third, the principal version of this passage is in Parashat Pinchas (folio 241a), for he said "and in the first composition" — the explanation in the Zohar being that it was the book prior to this one; and there in Parashat Pinchas he did not elaborate, neither in full nor in part, but only the beginning of the passage. And these are its words: "'I have gathered my myrrh with my spice' — the right arm with the left thigh; 'my honeycomb with my honey' — Jacob with Rachel; 'my wine with my milk' — the left arm with the right thigh." Thus far its words. And although he elaborated there on the matter of the mediation, [with] the appellation "my myrrh" which is Chesed, and "my spice" Netzach, as expounded — nevertheless regarding the explanation of the words he did not elaborate further. And one must consider why he did not adopt this correspondence here. Fourth, in his saying "Jacob with Rachel," he did not say "the body (gufa) with the female (nukva)," in the manner and correspondence of the limbs that he attributed to the other Sefirot. Fifth, after he set out to explain his words by saying "and these are," etc., it would have been fitting for him to say "the right arm with the left thigh — Chesed with Hod," for this is the correct order, and not to put the interpretation before the [scriptural] phrase by saying "Chesed with Hod — the right arm with the left thigh," etc., and so for all of them. Sixth, that which he found difficult — "and why are the attributes thus [crossed]?" — what is the difficulty? For sometimes Netzach draws sustenance from Gevurah, and likewise Hod from Chesed, even though most of their nourishment is Netzach from Chesed and Hod from Gevurah. For sometimes it happens, according to the blendings and the emanations, that Netzach draws from Gevurah and Hod from Chesed; and therefore each one is composed of all of them, so that they all agree to one action and one effluence. And therefore it is possible for two opposites to be equalized, even Gevurah with Chesed. And we shall explain that Rashbi, peace be upon him, found difficulty in the verse: for it would have been fitting to say "I have gathered my myrrh and my spice, I have eaten my honeycomb and my honey, I have drunk my wine and my milk" — why "with...with" (im, im)? For it is superfluous. To this he answered that there, above the passage before us (printed in Parashat Vayikra, folio 4b — see there), he said: "my myrrh with my spice" — Chesed with Netzach; "my honeycomb with my honey" — Gevurah with Hod; "my wine with my milk" — body and covenant (guf u-brit).

Now by this our question is partly resolved: that he said "with...with" in order to unite these attributes in the aforementioned manner. But because this answer is not sufficient — since the verse's intent is only to unite Chesed with Netzach, Gevurah with Hod, and Tiferet with Yesod — and nevertheless he could have been silent about "with...with," and it would be understood on its own that he means they are united, since this is their way, for three are united with three — therefore he said "and in the first composition" — explained in the Zohar in Parashat Pinchas — where another, more expansive interpretation is set forth, namely: "the right arm with the left thigh," the intent being that Chesed, despite its being the line of Chesed, is united with Hod, despite its being the line of Din. And likewise Gevurah, despite its being the line of Din, is united with Netzach, despite its being the line of Chesed. And now there is no difficulty as to why he said "with...with," for it was necessary because this is not their usual way. And since it is the reverse of their custom and nature, he therefore needed to say "with...with" in order to inform us of the reversal of this order. And the reason the Zohar spoke in the language of the appellations of the limbs — "thighs and arms" — and not the attributes by their names, is that he found difficulty: since he interpreted the Sefirot as reversed, contrary to their order, that is an impossible thing. For the manner of Netzach's nourishment is from the right, and likewise it is beneath Chesed, the line of Chesed; and the manner of Hod's nourishment is from the left, and likewise it is beneath Gevurah, the line of Din. And how is it possible that they should change their function? For this is impossible. And in order to explain this matter to us with a forceful figure of speech, he employed the language "thighs and arms," to tell you: that just as the thighs and the arms are joined together and connected with the body, and by means of the body it unites the right arm with the left thigh, and likewise the left arm with the right thigh — the central body being what unites and couples them together — so too is the matter above, by means of Tiferet, which branches out into the six extremities, and the extremities are its limbs; just as the limbs are branches to the body, so the extremities are limbs and branches to Tiferet. And therefore, by means of it, it is possible for these Sefirot to be blended in this blending, and it is within possibility and not among the impossible. And nevertheless we have not yet been saved from the question "why are His attributes thus [crossed]?," as we shall explain.

Now the reason has been explained why he was compelled to say "thighs and arms" and not the attributes themselves by their names. But Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Ra'aya Mehemna intended to bring the language of the first composition by quoting its very wording, which is: "I have gathered my myrrh with my spice — the right arm with the left thigh; my honeycomb with my honey — Jacob with Rachel; my wine with my milk — the left arm with the right thigh." Thus far the [first] composition. And he elaborated in explaining the rest of the passage. The intent is to explain to us the fine precision of his language in saying "the right arm with the left thigh," etc. — that the matter is not by way of happenstance, but, with precise intent, that Chesed unites with Hod and not [that] Hod unites with Chesed. That is to say: that the dwelling of Chesed shall be in Hod, and the principal one shall be Chesed; and likewise Gevurah, that its dwelling and seat shall be in Netzach, and the principal one shall be Gevurah (a variant reads "Netzach"), and not the reverse. And likewise Tiferet within Malkhut below. For if we were to say that the principal one is above — the lower [Sefirot subsumed] within the upper — the reason for "why are the attributes thus [crossed]?" would not be settled. For then it would emerge that the bride and her attendants ascend to the house of the groom and his attendants. And then it would not be fitting for the bride to change the customs of the groom at all, since she is lodging in his house. Rather, this is correct: Chesed within Hod, Gevurah within Netzach, Tiferet within Malkhut; and these are three upper [Sefirot] within three lower. Thus the groom lodges with his attendants in the house of the bride with her attendants; and since he is in the bride's house, it is fitting that he conduct himself according to the bride's will, and it is in her power to change the custom according to her will, as is better in her eyes. And with this there is an answer to the question "why are the attributes thus [crossed]?," etc., as we shall explain, God willing. And this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, intended in explaining to us the precision of his language, by placing the interpretation of the passage before the passage itself, saying "Chesed with Hod — the right arm with the left thigh," and not the reverse — to alert us to the precision of his language: that with deliberate intent he employed the idiom of "thighs and arms" and not the idiom of the attributes "Chesed and Hod," etc., to teach that this blending is by means of the body. And this he intended by placing the term "Chesed and Hod" before "arm and thigh," as if saying "scrutinize!" — for it would have been possible to be brief and say "Chesed and Hod," the idiom of the attributes, and not the idiom of the limbs; but rather to grant you understanding, that the secret of this blending — which seemingly appears reversed — is set aright by means of the body, which is the central Tiferet, as he explained. And on the contrary, "arm and thigh" is an explanation of "Chesed and Hod," and not [that] "Chesed and Hod" is an explanation of "arm and thigh." And by this we resolve [the fourth point]: that with Jacob and Rachel he did not need to change their names to the names of the bodily limbs, for their matter and their union involves no reversal but is as is customary in the world — Tiferet upon Malkhut — and therefore he did not change them.

And he further granted us understanding: that in the language of the first composition he said "the right arm with the left thigh," and likewise "the left arm with the right thigh," and did not say "with...with" but stated it concisely; whereas in this passage, in his explanation, he interpreted "Chesed with Hod," etc., and said "with...with." "And why are His attributes thus [crossed]?" — the explanation: granted, if we were to interpret that there is no reversal of the attributes except with regard to emanation and nourishment alone — that is, what had occurred to our mind in explaining "the right arm with the left thigh," that its intent is only regarding the effluence, that Chesed emanates into Hod and likewise that Gevurah emanates into Netzach — then it would not be difficult for us at all, for this is the way of the attributes, that these draw from those. But according to what he explained in this passage, "the right arm with the left thigh" means "with" in the full sense — that is, that Chesed unites below within Hod, and Gevurah below within Netzach — then it is difficult: why are the attributes thus [crossed]? For by way of actual union, this is not the way of the union of the Sefirot, since Netzach binds with Chesed and Hod with Gevurah, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Thigh of Jacob, God willing, in chapters 3 [and] 4. And the matter is: with regard to emanation, even though Chesed emanates into Hod, nevertheless Hod performs its action, which is the action of Din — even if it does not act with the same force as at the time of its drawing from Gevurah — and there is no concern in this, since there is no reversal in the attributes. But in actual union there is concern, because the action of Din is nullified entirely. For when [Gevurah] wishes to act with the judgment of Gevurah, Netzach will subdue that judgment and not allow it to act, in the secret of the union. And therefore it is difficult: why are the attributes thus [crossed]? For this is a reversal of the attributes and a blocking of judgment, and this is not fitting. And this is the "it is not the way of the world" said to David. And He answered, "for the sake of David Your servant," etc.: He changed [the order] and drew down the power of Rachamim. For even the "song of joy" (rinah), which is from the side of Din, as is known, He wished to be from the side of Chesed; and this will be explained further in the Gate of Essence and Governance, God willing, in chapter 6. And likewise the matter with Tiferet: since it comes to the house of Malkhut, as it says, "I have come into My garden, My sister, [My] bride" [Song of Songs 5:1], it is therefore fitting for it to conduct itself according to her will, even to reversing the attributes, in order to draw down the power of Rachamim all the more. And this is what is said: Chesed within Hod, Gevurah within Netzach, and Jacob within Rachel — for they are three upper [Sefirot] within three lower, by means of Jacob the groom who comes to the house of his bride Rachel, as we explained. But if the bride were ascending to the house of the groom, it would not be fitting to change [the order], for it is not the way of the world to change.
Now the explanation of the passage is complete, and we have derived good reason and knowledge that Tiferet also mediates between Gedulah and Hod, and between Gevurah and Netzach.

Since in the previous chapter we established, from the aforementioned passage, that Tiferet mediates between Gedulah and Hod and between Gevurah and Netzach — and the matter is somewhat strange to the listening ear — we have resolved to establish this topic further and to make the matters intelligible, to show that they are not far from reason nor strange, for the matter is very close to us. The matter is in what is well known: that Tiferet receives from Gedulah and Gevurah and emanates into Netzach and Hod. And there is no doubt that what Tiferet emanates into Hod must contain, within that effluence, a portion of effluence from Gedulah, which Tiferet received from it, as we explained; and likewise what Tiferet emanates into Netzach must contain, within that effluence, a portion from Gevurah. And there is no doubt that the effluence emanated from Tiferet to Netzach and Hod will not be, in its blend, exactly as [Tiferet] received it from Gedulah and Gevurah. Rather, it is blended by means of Tiferet into an intermediate blend, equalized to Gedulah and to Hod, and likewise equalized to Netzach and Gevurah; and thus it emerges that this mediation is, in part, a constant thing. And sometimes it happens that Tiferet is compelled to have the principal part of its reception be from the judgment of Gevurah, in order to emanate into Netzach for the world's need of judgment — for retribution and the like. Or, because it received much from Gevurah, it emanates it into Netzach in order to sweeten the judgment. And likewise sometimes Tiferet receives much from the side of Chesed and emanates into Hod in order to sweeten Hod. And this blending, and the like, will be explained in the Gate of the Channels (Tzinorot), chapter 2, God willing; and the matters are plain to the understanding and straight to those who find knowledge. We shall add further instruction in this matter and establish it from that on which all the Geonim agreed concerning the colors of the Sefirot: that the color of Netzach is red inclining toward white, and the color of Hod is white inclining toward red.

Now regarding Netzach they explained that it is red inclining toward white: the explanation of the red is from its reception of the harsh judgment of Gevurah, by means of the mediating Tiferet, as explained; and because of this judgment it is red. But from the side of its abundant nourishment from Chesed — for there is its home — its inclination is toward white, to whiten the redness, to return it to white; and this is "inclining," for its intent is that most of it be white. And likewise the matter, in reverse, with Hod: for by its nourishment from Chesed, through Tiferet which equalizes and mediates between them, it is white. But because its principal nourishment is from the side of Gevurah — for there is its principal inclination and place — it must be inclining toward red, and it tips the Rachamim toward the side of Din.
Now it emerges, according to this, that Tiferet mediates by its color — which is of white and red — between Gedulah and Hod, and between Gevurah and Netzach.

And the matter of these colors will be explained in the Gate of the Colors, God willing. And praise and thanksgiving to the One who bestows good upon the guilty, who has dealt bountifully with us. "The Lord is God, and He has given us light" [Psalms 118:27], to establish this matter with three faithful witnesses: by the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, by the reasoning of the Kabbalah, and by the words of the Geonim. The sum of the matter: the places requiring mediation are five against five. Chokhmah against Binah, Gedulah against Gevurah — that is two against two; Gedulah against Hod, Gevurah against Netzach — that is two against two; together they are four against four. Further, Yesod mediates between Netzach and Hod, as will be explained in the Gate of the Mediators, chapter 4; thus they are five against five. However, the mediators between the five and the five are only two: Yesod and Tiferet. How so? Yesod [mediates] between Netzach and Hod; and Tiferet [mediates] between Gedulah and Gevurah, between Gedulah and Hod, between Gevurah and Netzach, and between Chokhmah and Binah — in a hidden mode of existence, in the secret of Da'at, as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate. And with this premise the Mishnah that we are explaining will be understood — that it said "five against five" — for in truth they are five against five, and "the covenant of union is set in the middle," for the mediators mediate and are set between the extremities. And "the word of the tongue" is Tiferet, and it is called "the word of the tongue" because, by means of Binah — which is the tongue — it ascends above to mediate between Chokhmah and Binah, in the secret of Da'at, as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate. And likewise by means of it [Binah] it mediates between Gedulah and Gevurah, as we explained in chapter 2; and "the word of the ma'or" is Yesod, the second mediator.

Now by this the matter is further settled, and what we asked is essentially resolved — that they are "five against five" and [with] the mediator they are eleven — for we are now not [dealing] with the count of the Sefirot but with the count of the mediation, as explained; and there is no need to elaborate.

Now we have explained this Mishnah according to the most well-known version in the books and among the commentators. Although it appears that Nachmanides (the Ramban), peace be upon him, had a different reading, nevertheless we shall be concerned only with the consensus of most of the books. And when the student looks at the variant readings, he will find this reading to be more precise; and furthermore, it has not yet been verified that that interpretation is the Ramban's, as appears from an examination of it.

After we have journeyed from the mountain of the Lord — the high and steep mountain that is the previous Mishnah, in which we established the consensus of the Kabbalists that the Sefirot are ten and no more — let us go to the "mountain of myrrh," the second Mishnah relative to it, though it is the fourth from the head of the chapter. And these are its words: "Ten Sefirot of belimah: ten and not nine; ten and not eleven. Understand with wisdom (havein be-chokhmah), and be wise with understanding (chakam be-vinah). Test them and probe from them, and know and reckon from them; and set the matter in its clarity, and restore the Former (Yotzer) to His place." End of quote.

We have resolved not to raise any difficulties on this Mishnah at all, since its words are of themselves not [readily] ordered, and the text "demands to be expounded," and its surface meaning admits of no explanation, so that one must engage it in give-and-take. And we shall write what God places in our mouth concerning "ten and not nine" and its explanation. Namely, that his intent is to warn us against the error of saying that Keter is not among the Sefirot — for we might think it is the Ein Sof — which is not so. For "one high above another watches" [Ecclesiastes 5:7]. And [it is] not as many have thought, that the Ein Sof is among the count of the Sefirot and that it is Keter. And this opinion we shall refute in the Gate of "Whether the Ein Sof is Keter," God willing — and may the Merciful One save us from this opinion. Rather, certainly they are ten apart from the Emanator; for otherwise the emanated Sefirot would be nine, and this is not fitting. Rather, the emanated [Sefirot] themselves are ten and not nine. He further explained that [the Mishnah] comes to warn us not to err by separating Malkhut from the count — as there is one who supposed in his reasoning something close to this — and may the Merciful One also save us from this opinion. Rather, it is with them in Atzilut; and even though it is not in their unity, because it was driven out, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Diminishment of the Moon, God willing. And close to this explanation, Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Parashat Teitzei, folio 277b), whose words are: "And there are others, masters of Scripture, masters of [the] attributes, who inherit souls from the side of the holy Malkhut, which is composed of ten Sefirot — for whoever inherits it and merits it, merits the ten Sefirot without separation. 'Ten and not nine,' for if they were to inherit Malkhut as a single one [in isolation], they would be nine, separated from it; and because there is no separation there, the author of the Sefer Yetzirah said 'ten and not nine.' And should you say that it ascends above [beyond] ten — the explicit Name is spelled 'Yod-Heh, Vav-Heh,' behold, ten; the yod that unites with it does not ascend above ten; and therefore 'ten and not eleven.'" End of quote.

The intent of this passage, which said "and there are others": for above, in [the context of] this matter, he said that among the men of [pious] deeds there is one who has a soul (neshamah) which is a "handmaid" (amah) from the side of Beriah — and this matter will be explained in the Gate of the Soul, God willing. And now he said that there are others, "masters of Scripture" (marei sifra de-orayta), who are those engaged in the divine Torah and its secrets. And because it might have been said that "masters of Scripture" refers to those engaged in the depths of the laws, homilies, aggadot, statutes, judgments, and ordinances according to the plain sense alone — to this he said that, although the reward of these is doubled and redoubled, and it is the choice portion, nevertheless they do not merit the level of this [particular] soul until they reach the secrets of the Sefirot, which are the secret of the Godhead. And these are called "masters of [the] attributes" (marei middot); they are so called because all the engagement of the sages of Kabbalah is in the attributes and their matters. And he said that these inherit a soul from the side of Malkhut itself, not from the side of Metatron the servant, nor from the side of the "handmaid" (amah) mentioned there. And he said that one merits a soul composed of ten. And because he found difficulty — perhaps the other souls too are composed of ten, or perhaps this soul is not composed of ten; and whence have we the power to distinguish between one soul and another, even though this one is more esteemed than that — to this he establishes that, with [regard to] Malkhut, he means: the soul that is from the side of Malkhut is necessarily composed of ten, for the reason that the Sefirot do not separate but are bound and unified; and when we say "Malkhut," it is necessary that the other Sefirot be attached to it. Which is not so with a soul from the side of Metatron or the handmaid, for they are of the world of separation, since they descend from [below] Atzilut. And this necessity applies only in Atzilut and not to them; and therefore [such a soul] would not be composed of ten — only a soul from the side of Malkhut. And what we say — that the soul from the side of Metatron or the handmaid is not composed of ten — the intent is not that ten are not included in it, in the literal sense. For this is impossible: that there be an action drawn down from above that is not composed of all ten, for then separation would appear. And this is the reason for those with blemishes — such as those lacking hands and the like — who are deficient and indicate, by the defect of their action, that they damaged in a holy place and caused separation; and therefore their soul does not spread through the body in those limbs, and it is blemished and deficient; and all according to the place of their damage, so is their blemish. And a blemish [present] from the beginning of one's creation indicates its deficiency on account of [a previous] transmigration (gilgul), as we shall explain the matter of the limbs in the Gate of the Soul, chapter 7, God willing. And it is never possible in the world [for there to be] a soul or an action in which all ten Sefirot are not included. And although it is declared "a soul from the side of Metatron, or from the side of the handmaid," the intent is not that they are not from above, God forbid — for all souls are drawn down from above. And the matter is as we shall explain in the aforementioned Gate, chapter 2, God willing; and it is always composed of ten, and they do not separate, as explained. And [the difference] between souls from Malkhut and the other souls is this: that the other souls are composed of ten — not that ten actually appear in them, but rather that they are included in it [Malkhut], and it of itself is composed of ten. But the soul from the side of Malkhut is emanated from the ten Sefirot that are in Malkhut, in that Malkhut has all ten Sefirot appearing within it and unites with them.

And this matter will be further explained in the coming Gates, God willing. And this matter [applies] to the Sefirot themselves: for there is a great difference between our saying "Malkhut is composed of ten" and our saying that it is in union with the very essences of the other Sefirot, for they are not all one [and the same] thing. For the excellence of a Sefirah when it is [merely] composed [of ten] is not like its excellence when it is united with the very essences of the Sefirot — which is when ten Sefirot actually appear within it — and this is clear. And this is what he intended in saying "composed of ten Sefirot." And he clarified that the intent in saying "composed" is not that it is merely composed [of ten], as is the usual nature of the Sefirot, but rather that "whoever inherits it," etc., "merits ten Sefirot without separation" — meaning that one truly merits the ten Sefirot in their [actual] existence, in that ten Sefirot actually appear within it, as explained.

And the matter of his saying "who inherits it and merits it": the explanation is that two things are needed in order to merit this esteemed soul. First, from the side of his preparation — from the side of his father at the time of begetting, at the time of [marital] union — as the Sages said, "one who sanctifies himself at the time of intercourse," etc.; and after his father is sanctified thereby, when that good intention of his ascends, he will merit a holy soul from a high place; and according to the measure of his sanctity, so will his drawing-down be elevated. And this is well known in the Zohar and the Talmud in many places, too numerous to count. And their saying "he merits worthy children" — the intent is that he draws down for his children a soul from a high place, such that they will be worthy; and this is called "inheritance from his father," and to this he referred in saying "who inherits it." Second, one needs in himself worthy deeds, pleasing before his Maker, so that that soul will not depart from him; and this will be explained further in the Gate of the Soul, chapter 3, God willing. And concerning this second [thing] he said "and merits it" — meaning that he is the one who, by his deeds, merits that holy soul. "He merits ten Sefirot without separation" — meaning, as we explained, that when the soul is from the essence of Malkhut, then necessarily that soul will be "composed of ten Sefirot," meaning of the very essence of the ten Sefirot within it, because it unites with the ten Sefirot and is not separated from them at all. And this is what he said, "he merits ten Sefirot without separation" — that is, [they are] unified within Malkhut, not separated from it. And he established this from the words of the Sefer Yetzirah, which said "ten and not nine." And if it were possible to say that the soul could be separated — the soul which is necessarily a part of Malkhut, as it says, "and He breathed into his nostrils" (Genesis 2:7); whoever breathes, breathes from his own essence — then [what happens] by way of the part would happen to the whole: for just as the soul drawn from it [Malkhut] would be separated from the other parts of the Sefirot, so Malkhut would be separated, God forbid, from the other Sefirot. And this is impossible, for then the Sefirot would remain nine; therefore he said "ten and not nine," that they never diminish from ten. And therefore the soul must, besides being composed of ten, have the very essences of the Sefirot included within it, exactly as Malkhut [does], for whatever is in the part is in the whole. "And should you say that it ascends above," etc. — the explanation: he found difficulty in that one might say they [the Sefirot] are ten apart from Malkhut, and according to this it would be possible to say that Malkhut is separated from the rest and yet they are ten. To this he answered, "the explicit Name (shem mefarash)," etc. The explanation: the explicit Name is the four-letter Name, YHVH, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Four-Letter Name; and this Name is in the attribute of Tiferet, and it is the male that unites with Malkhut, which is the female, and it unites with her. And this Name indicates, in its full spelling, that it is a "private domain" (reshut ha-yachid), its height ten and its breadth four — which is YHVH, and this is its breadth; and its height is ten: Yod-Heh, Vav-Heh, behold ten, for it never ascends above ten. And if it were that they were ten apart from Malkhut, then when the Name unites with Malkhut they would be eleven — ten above and one that unites with the female; therefore the Sefer Yetzirah said "ten and not eleven."

Now the explanation of the passage is complete, and we have written, in passing, the explanation of the Mishnah, "ten and not nine and not eleven." We may also explain "ten and not eleven" [as follows]: he intended to warn us not to bring into the count of the emanated [entities] the Throne, which is an appellation for Beriah, as we shall explain in the Gate of ABiYA, God willing. And likewise he intended to warn us not to bring into the count of the emanated [entities] the angel, the Prince of the Countenance, Metatron — for although his name is like the name of his Master, he is only of [the world of] Yetzirah and not Atzilut, as we shall explain in the aforementioned Gate, God willing. And all these interpretations [arise] in explaining the Mishnah, since it spoke in the language of affirmation and negation: "ten" is affirmation, and "not nine" is negation; likewise "ten and not eleven." And his intent is to affirm this number, which is ten, and to negate every kind of error that adds to the ten or diminishes from them.

They further explained for us another interpretation of this Mishnah in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Parashat Tisa, folio 187b), whose words are: "A commandment to give the half-shekel in the sacred shekel. Said the Faithful Shepherd: What is the half-shekel? It is like the half of the hin; and this is the vav, mediating between the two hehs. 'A stone with which to weigh' — this is yod; 'twenty gerah is the shekel' — this is the [spelled-out] yod. 'The rich shall not give more' — this is the central pillar; it shall not exceed ten. For so it is said in the Sefer Yetzirah: 'Ten Sefirot of belimah; ten and not eleven.' 'And the poor shall not give less' — this is the Tzaddik; it shall not be less than ten, as it says, 'ten and not nine'; and the half-shekel — it is ten." End of quote.

There are points to scrutinize in this passage. First, his saying "What is the half-shekel? It is like the half," etc. — the explanation being that "half the hin" is Tiferet, which mediates between the two hehs. However, with regard to "the half-shekel," it is not apt to interpret thus — "mediating between" — for we do not know between what [it would mediate]. Second, his saying "a stone with which to weigh — this is yod," etc.: here, according to the implication, the [spelled-out] yod is twenty. And how did he say that one must not subtract from nor add to the ten — behold, the [spelled-out] yod, whose half is ten, and behold it has added ten to ten, which is twenty? And according to his explanation, one must not add to the ten in any Sefirah — for [it is] not specifically Tiferet or the Tzaddik, but he took these [as examples] because they are "rich" and "poor," and all the more so the others. Third, his saying "a stone with which to weigh — this is yod" — how does one weigh with this stone, given that it is twenty gerah, while the weight needs to be in ten, which is only the half-shekel? And if we say that his intent is to speak of the manner of weighing with this stone — which is the whole stone — then it is prolix, and it would have been fitting for him to say "a stone with which to weigh — this is the [spelled-out] yod, and it is twenty gerah." Why did he say "a stone with which to weigh — this is yod; twenty gerah is the shekel — this is the [spelled-out] yod," which is repetitive and prolix? Fourth, his saying "and the half-shekel — it is ten," which appears to have no connection.

And further, that it is the opposite of what he explained: for above he said that the explanation of "half-shekel" is "mediating," and now he says "the half-shekel — it is ten," which implies that "half" is [literally] half of a shekel, in its [plain] sense.

Now to understand this passage we must first premise that the matter of the Sefirot is [that they are] ten from above to below and ten from below to above — like the image of a ray of the sun that comes and strikes a polished mirror, and the light returns and reverses back toward its source; so it is with the Sefirot, for they come from above to below until Malkhut, and there is the "station" of the light, and it returns to its source by way of the journeys, such that just as they are ten from above to below, so they are ten from below to above. And this topic we shall elaborate upon in the appropriate Gate, God willing.

Now this secret is made clear from the form of the [letter] alef, which is a yod above and a yod below, to indicate the source of the light from above to below and from below to above; and these are the "upper waters" and the "lower waters," as we shall explain in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions, under the heading "water," God willing.

Now the vav that is in the middle of the two yods is Tiferet, which unites the upper waters and the lower waters; and this is the half-shekel, which mediates within the shekel — which is the complete measure, the measure of Atzilut: ten from above to below and ten from below to above — and it is mediating and central between the two yods, which are "twenty gerah is the shekel." And now the meaning of "half the hin" and the meaning of "half the shekel" are all one [and the same] thing. And the first difficulty is resolved. "A stone with which to weigh — this is yod": the explanation is that a "stone" is always the form of yod, which is called "stone," and every "stone" is alluded to in the existence of yod, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions, under the heading "stone," God willing.

Now it is a "stone" with which to weigh the half-shekel, for the half-shekel is ten, as we shall explain; and therefore the "stone" with which one weighs is the form of yod, and this is ten. "Twenty gerah is the shekel — this is the [spelled-out] yod": the explanation of what he said, "twenty gerah is the shekel — this is yod" [in its full spelling], is that it indicates twenty, which is the two yods — ten from above to below [and] ten from below to above.

Now its half, which is the simple [unspelled] yod, is the "stone" for weighing; and when it is full [spelled out] it is a whole shekel, which is twenty gerah — ten from above to below and ten from below to above, as we explained. "The rich shall not give more — this is the central pillar; it shall not exceed ten," etc. The explanation: needless to say [regarding] the other Sefirot, but even the "rich" one — which is rich in effluence and in inclusion more than the other Sefirot — nevertheless may not add inclusiveness beyond ten Sefirot, because they are ten and not eleven. And so it may not add inclusiveness beyond ten on account of its richness; rather, its richness will be in an abundance of effluence and light, or in its being composed of many tenfold compositions, but it will never add to the inclusion of ten. "And the poor shall not give less — this is the Tzaddik; it shall not be less than ten," etc. The explanation: Yesod — although it is called "poor" on account of its poverty [in the time of exile], as it says (Isaiah 57:1), "the righteous one perishes," etc., and it is poor and destitute — he said that, although it is poor, its poverty is not [such as] to fall below ten Sefirot at all, for one must not fall short of them, in the sense of "ten and not nine"; rather, its poverty is in the diminution of its effluence or the diminution of [its] composition of the ten, but not that it falls short of them — only that it does not add many compositions [each] of tenfold ten. But from the aforementioned ten one must not subtract, so that there not be less than ten; for it is impossible to say that there be a place devoid [of the ten] in any one of them — rather, they are always ten. "And the half-shekel — it is ten." The explanation: now, according to what we explained — that the "rich" one is the central pillar, which is truly the half-shekel, mediating between the two yods which are a shekel of twenty gerah — then the half-shekel is ten, and ten is the half-shekel. And so, since the verse comes to teach us that the "rich" one, which is Tiferet, must not add beyond ten — then how did he say "the rich shall not give more than the half-shekel," when it [Tiferet] is itself the half-shekel? And how did he give a measure to the "rich" one, which is Tiferet, by [reference to] the half-shekel, which is Tiferet itself? To this he said, "and the half-shekel — it is ten." The explanation: although we explained above that Tiferet is the one called "half-shekel" because it is intermediate — with all this, "a verse does not depart from its plain sense": it is called thus by its aspect of being within the shekel and dividing it in two, and half the shekel is ten. And now he said: the "rich" one shall never add, in its existence which is [that of] the half-shekel — that is, that it divides the shekel into two and makes each of them ten by ten. Thus far the explanation of the passage. And we find ourselves learning from it the explanation of the Mishnah, that "ten and not nine, ten and not eleven" comes to teach us concerning the matter of the inclusion of [things] included — that one must not add to ten, as explained.

And now let us return to explaining the rest of the language of the Mishnah, which said "Understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding," etc. The commentators explained that the intent is to unite Chokhmah with Binah and Binah with Chokhmah. They further explained that the intent is to convey that the root of Chokhmah is in Binah and the root of Binah is in Chokhmah. They further explained: when you draw effluence to Chokhmah, let it be on condition that it come to Binah; and when you draw [effluence] to Binah, give it the power of Chokhmah. And according to these matters and the like the commentators explained, but their explanation is not settled. For why would [the Mishnah] now warn us about these matters with Binah and Chokhmah and not with the other Sefirot? For surely, just as we are obligated to unite the first three, so we are obligated to unite the seven that are below them.

And further: why does Keter not enter into this matter of union, according to some of the interpretations? Further, [the Mishnah] said "test them," etc., and the commentators explained that when you test [them] well you will know that the aforementioned Chokhmah and Binah are the root of Gedulah and Gevurah; and "probe from them" means: when you probe, you will find that Gedulah and Gevurah are the root of Netzach and Hod, which extend from them. And he said "and set the matter (davar) in its clarity (boryo)": "davar" [is] Malkhut; "boryo" is like "its support," and so Onkelos translated (Exodus 21:19), and it is Yesod. "And restore the Former (Yotzer) to His place (mekhono)": "restore" (hashev) corresponds to teshuvah [Binah], to give its power to Tiferet, which is designated by the name "Former" (Yotzer); and the "place" of Tiferet is Netzach and Hod. Thus far the words of the commentators, after we have selected the choicest and finest of their interpretations. And since this matter is not settled for us — because this is not the nature of an author's language; and furthermore, what is the point of informing us now of these matters and these novel teachings? For this is the way of those who pray, not of authors, and we derive from this no instruction or novelty — therefore it seems to me to explain that "chokhmah" is the received tradition and learning that a person learns from his teacher, in the sense of "they transmit to him the headings of the chapters [outlines]." "Binah" is the analysis and the addition that a person studies out and adds of himself, from the general principles and chapter-headings transmitted to him. And now to this they referred in saying "Understand with wisdom" (havein be-chokhmah) — that is, study well what you learned from your teacher in the wisdom of the attributes, in which only chapter-headings are transmitted; and a person needs to understand from it one matter [derived] from another, in the sense of what the Sages said (Chagigah 13a): "one does not say this matter except to a sage who understands of his own knowledge."

Behold, [this means] that a person needs to liken one matter to another and to derive one matter from another, so that he will have a "generative intellect" (sechel molid) and not a "barren intellect" (sechel akar). And he said "be wise with understanding" (chakkem be-vinah) — the explanation: when you generate and liken in your intellect and understand, you must "make it wise" and ground it in the received tradition of the masters and in the brevity of their words, so that the matter is included in what is transmitted to you, whether much or little; "and do not lean upon your own understanding" [Proverbs 3:5]. "Test them" (bechon bahem) — that is, with regard to the very essence of the Sefirot, that is, "in them," in their quiddity, the examination shall be only by way of "running and returning" (ratzo va-shov) and by way of humility, being mindful of the honor of your Maker, who makes the simple wise; and this is "in them." But with regard to the actions that proceed from them, the matter shall be [pursued] with intense investigation, with good knowledge, with give-and-take, and with great study. And since investigation is into the actions that proceed to us from the existence of the Sefirot, he said "probe from them" (chakor me-hem) — meaning, into what proceeds from them, and not into their essence, which is "in them," as he said above. "And set the matter in its clarity" — the explanation: establish the matter firmly and descend to the depth of the topic, so that it will be clear to you without doubt. "And restore the Former to His place" — the explanation: in any case, let your entire intent be that the King of kings, the Ein Sof, blessed be He, oversee from His "place," which are His thrones, which are the ten Sefirot; and the intent is that all be [directed] toward the matter of the union of the emanated [Sefirot], which unite in the Emanator, and the Emanator in the emanated. Or he means "set the matter in its clarity" in the manner that the commentators explained — that is, the union of Malkhut with Yesod, and not to separate them by believing [there to be] nine, God forbid, but rather ten together with Malkhut. "And restore the Former to His place" — for the Sefirot are a "place" and a throne for Him, and He is the Lord, the Emanator, like a king upon the throne, and He is not among the count of the "throne." Thus far the explanation of the Mishnah.

Now it has been explained from these chapters that the Sefirot are ten, neither less nor more, and there is no doubt in this matter, God forbid; rather it is a belief [held] in the heart of all the Kabbalists.

After we have engaged, in the previous chapters, in the strengthening of our beliefs — agreed upon by all the Kabbalists — that the Sefirot are ten, neither less nor more, we have seen fit in this chapter to save the student from a place of confusion and error; and it is a question that was asked of Rav Hai Gaon. And these are the words of the questioners: "Let our master teach us — for we find that the Sages [speak of] thirteen attributes [of mercy] that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, received; and for Abraham our father, peace be upon him, in a book that the Sages attributed to his name — which is the Sefer Yetzirah — there [the author] counts ten Sefirot. And we need to learn from his holy mouth whether the ten Sefirot are the thirteen attributes. If so, we find thirteen attributes [but] we do not find thirteen Sefirot; or [are there] thirteen attributes alone and ten Sefirot alone? We are in need of your instruction, and we await your answer." End of quote of the question.

Now the master [Rav Hai] explained to them that the thirteen attributes are derivative branches issuing from the ten levels called Sefirot, these corresponding to those, together with three hidden ones, "heads of heads." "And if they are not [evident] to you as [distinct] entities, there is a tradition concerning them [handed down] by our predecessors, each from the mouth of the other, up to the mouth of the prophets, of blessed memory"; and the derivatives — which are the actions — are called "attributes" (middot), and the roots, which are "fathers," are called "Sefirot," not because there is [merely a] number, etc. And we shall not copy the entire text of his answer, because we are destined to copy it and explain it at length in the Gate of the Resplendences (Tzachtzachot), chapter 1, God willing. And now it is fitting that we say that the master's intent, in saying "together with three heads of heads," etc., is not that his answer to them is that there are thirteen Sefirot. For if this were his intent, he would have had to resolve for them the essence of their question — namely, that [the statement] in the Sefer Yetzirah, "ten and not eleven," is not the [accepted] law. And since we see that the Gaon was not concerned to reconcile the wording nor to reject it, it appears that he indicates that the three hidden ones are not Sefirot, such that we should say they are thirteen. For they are only hidden powers — an existence subtler than the existence of the Sefirot — as we shall expand upon there, God willing. And just as we have no difficulty from finding that there are ten of Atzilut, ten of Beriah, ten of Yetzirah, and ten of Asiyah, so the existence of the hidden ones poses no difficulty to us, because the Sefirot are never anything but ten. And if we find hidden entities, they are sources for the revealed ones; and if there are revealed ones, they are a shadow to the upper ones; and they never ascend above ten nor descend below ten; and the three are sources, as we shall explain there in the exposition of the Gaon's words, God willing. There is further room for error in the Baraita of Rabbi Shimon HaTzaddik, which Rav Chamai Gaon copied in the Book of Contemplation (Sefer ha-Iyyun) that he composed, whose words are: "And these are thirteen powers, each of which has a known name, and the name of their rank, one above the other: (1) Primordial Air (avir kadmon); (2) Primeval Wisdom (chokhmah kedumah); (3) Wondrous Light (or mufla); (4) Chashmal; (5) Arafel [dense cloud]; (6) the Throne of Radiance (kisei ha-nogah); (7) the Wheel (ofan) of Greatness, called Chazchazit, the place from which the vision of the seers issues; (8) Cherub (keruv); (9) the Wheels (galgalei) of the Chariot; (10) the Encompassing Air (avir ha-sovev); (11) the Curtain (pargod) — this is the Throne of Glory; (12) the place of the souls, called the Chambers of Greatness; (13) the secret of the supernal array (ma'arakhah), called the supernal Sanctuary of Holiness. And these thirteen powers are revealed as one, from the hidden supernal Keter, called Omman (Artisan)," etc. End of quote, as relevant to our matter. And in truth, seemingly it implies that he is enumerating the order of the Sefirot, and so it is — that the Sefirot are ten. The first, "Primordial Air," is Keter, for so its name is well known, as will be explained in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions; (2) "Primeval Wisdom" is, literally, Chokhmah; (3) "Wondrous Light" is Binah; (4) "Chashmal" is Chesed; (5) "Arafel" is Gevurah; (6) "the Throne of Radiance" is Tiferet; (7) "Chazchazit" is Netzach, and it is one of the [sources of] true prophecy; (8) "Cherub" is Hod; (9) "the Wheel of the Chariot" is Yesod; (10) "the Encompassing Air" is Malkhut. From here onward [the list] is not among the Sefirot but [consists of] levels that are below the Sefirot. And some have explained that they are three kinds of "emanation" within Malkhut, and not actual Atzilut. But it seems to us that his intent is that they are three hidden sources within Malkhut — for the allusion came in it [Malkhut]: just as three hidden upper ones are alluded to in Keter, so they came in it [Malkhut] revealed; and this is not the place for this matter, but rather the Gate of the Resplendences and the Gate of ABiYA, God willing. And as for the three extra [items] in the words of Rabbi Shimon HaTzaddik, peace be upon him — which are (11) Curtain (pargod), (12) the place of the souls called the Chambers of Greatness, (13) the secret of the supernal array called the supernal Sanctuary of Holiness — it appears to us, from his language, when examined with good study, that he is not speaking of the matter of the Sefirot but [of] the powers of the Sefirot; and in particular, that he called the eleventh "Curtain" (pargod), the meaning of which is "a place of division," and it is a partition and screen between Atzilut and the other things below Atzilut; and he called it "the Throne of Glory," which is a throne that comprises many thrones, and which is, for us, the matter designated by the term "Beriah," as will be explained in the Gate of ABiYA, God willing.

Now it is known that the souls are hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory; and although in truth they are emanated from above the Throne, nevertheless they are hewn from beneath the Throne — for "hewing" is an appellation for Yetzirah, as we shall explain in the aforementioned Gate.

Now Yetzirah is beneath Beriah; thus the souls — the place of their hewing is beneath the Throne of Glory, that is, beneath Beriah; and therefore the level beneath the Throne of Glory is called "the place of the souls," and likewise "the Chambers of Greatness," which are, literally, the chambers of the Garden of Eden. And beneath this Yetzirah is Asiyah, which is designated by his language "the secret of the supernal array" — and they are the array of the ministering [angels] in the secret of Asiyah, who are beneath Yetzirah. This is what appears to us regarding the matter of the Baraita of Rabbi Shimon HaTzaddik.
