Now the matter of the thirteen attributes is settled, and according to both this one and that one, the Sefirot are never anything but ten. However, regarding the question they asked the Gaon — whether the thirteen attributes are Sefirot or not — we have a proof that they are not an allusion to the Sefirot, in line with the Gaon's reasoning. And the proof is that they are called "thirteen attributes of mercy (rachamim)," yet among the Sefirot there are attributes of Din, such as Gevurah and Hod. Therefore, what is clear to us in this is that the thirteen attributes are the twelve boundaries (gevulin), which are the twelve [permutations of the four-letter] Name (havayot), and they are twelve; and the place that bears them, which is the Name that comprises them, [together they] are thirteen. And they are in each of three places, which are Teli, Galgal (sphere), and Lev (heart), and the mnemonic is "TaGeL" [TGL]. Besides which there are yet another thirteen [attributes] that are hidden, and they are in Keter. And what is fitting to elaborate in explaining this topic will be explained in the Gate of the Particulars of the Names, God willing, for there is its place, in the exposition of the seventy-two-[letter] Name.

Now Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, peace be upon him, is [counted] among [those holding] this view, for he counted thirteen attributes in Keter, as I shall copy his words in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 3, God willing. And likewise Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Idra wrote of thirteen attributes of mercy in Ze'eir Anpin and thirteen attributes in Arikh Anpin. It certainly appears that their view is the opposite of the Gaon's view, of blessed memory. And the exposition of the thirteen attributes does not belong here, for it will be explained in a book of its own, if God decrees [for me] life. And our purpose in this is to uphold the belief of the Kabbalists: that one must not believe in any addition to the ten Sefirot nor in any [number] less than them — for it is "a tent that shall not be moved, whose stakes shall not be pulled up" [Isaiah 33:20] — ten and not eleven; and one who adds or diminishes sins and brings evil upon himself. And of God we ask that He save us from errors.

After we have verified the matter of the number of the Sefirot, it is fitting that we investigate whether they are necessary from the standpoint of inquiry or not. To this we say that they are necessary for several reasons. The first: because we who believe in providence — and even in particular providence — are compelled to say that He exercises providence by way of the Sefirot. For the simple One, the Cause of all causes and the Cause of Causes, is removed from change and from attributes — that is, "wise," "righteous," "one who hears," and the rest of the predicates that the philosophers have removed from Him. So too the dimensions of body and corporeality, such as "And YHVH came down," and "And the appearance of the glory of YHVH was like a consuming fire," etc., and "And I saw YHVH sitting upon a throne," etc., and "And the glory of YHVH filled the Tabernacle," and "And they saw the God of Israel, and under His feet," etc., and what is said in Daniel (7:9), "And the Ancient of Days sat; His garment was white as snow," and likewise "written with the finger of God," "the ears of YHVH," "the hand of YHVH," "the eyes of YHVH" — matters of this kind that occur in Scripture indicating limit and corporeality, and likewise indicating predicates. Now of the simple One, in respect of its aspect relative to its essence and its simplicity, it is impossible to say this — unless we consider it relative to its attributes, as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Vessels and in the Gate of Allusions, with the help of God.
And so it is by way of the attributes that the changes occur, and judgment and mercy — not in His [own] aspect — as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate.

Now from the standpoint of this aspect — so that we not deny the principles of our faith in the simple One, in the reality of its simplicity, that it is removed from the predicates that entail body and corporeal forms — and since we are compelled to believe in His providence, which too is among the principles of the religion, we therefore need to believe in the Sefirot, so that the principles of our faith not contradict one another, as explained. This, then, is a reason — or reasons — compelling belief in the Sefirot; and these are somewhat compelling proofs from the side of the Torah, by way of inquiry. However, by way of inquiry alone, without support and prop from the Torah, the commentators have written many further proofs; and because our way in this composition is not by way of inquiry, we have not copied them at all. Furthermore, these ten attributes — their secret and their import — have been expounded in Scripture. The first three are expounded from the words of Job to his companions, where he said (28:12), "But wisdom — whence shall it be found, and where is the place of understanding?" In this verse he set out for us the order of the first three, which are called Ayin (Nothing), Chokhmah, and Binah. First he said: Chokhmah is emanated from the first Sefirah, called Ayin, and this is "But wisdom — from Ayin (me-ayin) shall it be found." And A-Y — which is alef = Ayin, yod = Chokhmah — ZeH (this) is the place of Binah, [the place] by which Binah is emanated. But of the emanation of the Ayin he did not speak at all, for even the emanated is called Ayin (Nothing), all the more so the Emanator.

Now the seven [Sefirot] that proceed from them are expounded in the words of David, king of Israel, peace be upon him, in the verse (1 Chronicles 29:11): "Yours, O YHVH, is the greatness, and the power, and the beauty, and the victory, and the majesty; for all that is in heaven and on earth [is Yours]; Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom." The words "Yours, O YHVH" (lekha) are an epithet for the first three; and Binah is called lekha, which equals 50, like the count of the fifty gates of Binah. And the letters of L-KH (lekha) are the same as the letters of K-L (kol). And Yesod, when it receives from Binah the aforementioned fifty (nun) gates, is called KoL — like the image of the reversing seal, from L-KH to K-L. And the reason that the fifty gates are alluded to in the word lekha and in the word kol is that the gates are 50, in the secret of Binah, which spreads down to Hod — these being five Sefirot, each composed of ten, making fifty; and they are three over two: Gedulah-Gevurah-Tiferet (GGT) are a segol or segolta, which is 30; Netzach and Hod are a tzere or sheva, making 20 — thus L-KH (30+20) in their order. And KoL is in the secret of the reversing seal: what was above returned below. And the remaining matters of the gates will be explained in the Gate of Gates, with God's help. "The greatness" (ha-gedulah) is Chesed; "the power" (ha-gevurah) is Fear (Pachad); and then Tiferet, and Netzach, and Hod. "For all (kol) that is in heaven and on earth" — this is Yesod, the bond that binds heaven and earth. That is: it unifies Tiferet, called "heaven," and "earth," called Malkhut; and it is Yesod. And Malkhut was not clearly expounded in the verse; rather he said "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom" — because Malkhut's place is above Netzach, Hod, and Yesod, and on account of [its] diminishment it descended below. Therefore he did not wish to mention it except by way of the unification, to indicate that its place is in heaven, save that it was cast from heaven to earth; and afterward he said "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom," to set forth its hosts and its adornments in their own right; and even so he returned and unified it up to the supernal root, saying "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom" — "Yours" [referring to] Binah, as explained. "YHVH" is Tiferet. "The kingdom" (mamlakhah) is Malkhut, in its plain sense. And this is its mode of existence together with its spouse — two kings nourished from a single Keter.

After we have occupied ourselves in the preceding chapters with the necessity of the existence of the Sefirot and their number, it is fitting that we know whether one who denies the matter of the existence of the Sefirot is called a heretic [kofer] or not. And we say that a person's error in this matter will be in one of two ways. The first way: one who did not know of them at all — not in the sense that, were the hidden things of wisdom revealed to him, he would deny them, God forbid, but [only] in the sense that he was not habituated to them and the gates of light were not revealed to him. This man certainly ought not to be called a heretic [kofer] or a denier. And a proof of this: for even regarding the removal of corporeality from the truly simple One, blessed be He, Rambam said, in Sefer ha-Mada, in the Laws of Repentance ch.3, that one who believes the simple One is a body and possessed of form is a sectarian [min], and he included him in the category of the sectarians (minim). And Ra'avad, peace be upon him, objected to him, and these are his words: "I say: and why did he call this one a sectarian? — when several great and good men greater than he went with this thought, according to what they saw in the Scriptures, and even more than what they saw in the words of the aggadot, which confuse the views." So Ra'avad, peace be upon him, took issue with him for saying that one who says that God is a body is a sectarian. And it is not fitting to think that Ra'avad's view, peace be upon him, is that he is not a sectarian — for surely one who corporealizes God is a sectarian. Rather, their dispute hangs on this: that Rambam, according to the apparent sense of his language, holds that one who says that God is corporeal is a sectarian, even though this error stems from his not being habituated in divine matters, and from his having chased after the plain senses of the Scriptures and the midrashim, not descending into their depth to understand their matters as they truly are. And to this Ra'avad objected, of blessed memory, and contradicted him, and said that such a man — who in all his affairs serves God and walks in the ways of the Torah in innocence, and who, through the shortness of his knowledge, believed in corporeality — is not called a sectarian, though he certainly errs, since his intent is not to do evil, God forbid. But one who recognizes his Creator, to whom the gates of the premises in the removal of corporeality have been revealed, and who does not acknowledge the truth, but is brazen and says that God is a body — this one is surely called a sectarian, even according to the view of Ra'avad, of blessed memory. And likewise we say regarding the matter of the Sefirot: that surely one who did not know of them and believed in the simple One without knowledge of the Sefirot ought not to be called a heretic [kofer], God forbid, nor "one who cuts among the saplings" [mekatzetz ba-neti'ot], God forbid. For if so, it would have been fitting that, when a person is able to understand the training in the commandments, they should train him in the matter of belief in the Sefirot and the knowledge of them — which we do not find to be so. But on the contrary, they said that it is fitting to conceal them, and that these matters are transmitted only to the modest, etc. This is not so with the matter of the existence of God, and the unity, and the matter of Torah from Heaven, and the prophecy of Moses, and most of the principles of the religion: for when the lad knows how to call "my father" and "my mother," they train him in them and reveal to him the plain sense of the matters, as our Sages of blessed memory said in Tractate Sukkah (42a): once he knows how to speak, his father teaches him Torah and the Shema. And they asked in the Gemara, "What is 'Torah'?" and they said, "'Moses commanded us the Torah,' etc."; and "the Shema" is "Hear, O Israel," etc.

Now, they chose these two verses because in them are included most of the corners of the cardinal principles of the Torah. In the verse "Hear, O Israel" is included the existence of God — namely, "YHVH." Further, that He exercises providence, and even particular providence — and this is the meaning of "Eloheinu (our God)." For although His existence is necessary in respect of the whole world entire — and He was, is, and will be, and brings into being all the existents (which is the meaning of the four-letter Name in its writing); and although He is Master of all worlds, upper and lower (which is the meaning of its reading in lordship [Adonut]) — and from this His providence is necessitated as encompassing the whole world: even so, "Eloheinu" means that He watches over us in particular. "YHVH is One (echad)" necessitates the unity. And they have already explained in the Gemara (Berakhot 13b) that a person must intend, in the word echad, that He is King above and below and in the four directions. And by this it is necessitated that He is not a body, for the corporeal cannot be found in differing places at one time. Further, the meaning of echad: [it means] not like one of an enumeration, etc., as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Vessels, in Gate 4, ch.5, with the help of God. And in the verse "Moses commanded us the Torah" is included the cardinal principle of Torah from Heaven, and prophecy, and the prophecy of Moses — and this is "Moses commanded us the Torah," as is well known. Reward and punishment — in his saying "an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob," for YHVH desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make Israel meritorious and to bequeath them His Torah. And this is what they intended in saying these two verses: for the reason that, when the lad grows, he begins to roam in his thought among these words, and asks his father and his elder their reason and their matter; and they tell it to him and bring him into the matters of the corners of the Torah little by little, according to his understanding, as he is able to bear. This is what is found regarding the existence of the cardinal principles. Not so with the supernal Sefirot — on the contrary, they conceal their secret from every eye, and reveal them only to the modest, the unique ones in the generation. And here, then, is proof that one who does not discern the matter of the Sefirot is not, on this account, called a heretic [kofer], nor "one who cuts among the saplings," God forbid. Rather, what we may rightly say of him is that he did not merit to behold the luminaries in his days, nor tasted the sweetness of the Torah and the nectar of its pleasant sayings; and behold, he died without wisdom and saw no good. The second way: these are those to whom the matter of the Sefirot and their existence were revealed, and who deny them because of the evil of their disposition — for they were habituated in external sciences, and "with the children of strangers they content themselves." And these, even if they not be called heretics (koferim) or sectarians (minim), inasmuch as they believe in all the matters of divinity — even so they are called heretics (koferim), because they deny an interpretation of the Oral Torah. And one of the three [kinds of] heretics is one who denies an interpretation among the interpretations of the Oral Torah, as Rambam wrote in the aforementioned chapter; and he also denies the words of our Sages of blessed memory. And besides what is already his, he adds to his sin a transgression: for from the denial of the Sefirot, heresy will follow — for we will compel him by the premises and corners of the Torah: since the simple One is not subject to change, how does He watch over passing matters? And likewise, since He is one, how does He watch over the kinds of species — for that would necessitate multiplicity, as is known? And therefore he is compelled to believe in the Sefirot; and if not, he falls into heresy, God forbid — as many have erred in [the matter of] the removal of particular providence, and in these matters, which it is not fitting to raise up in writing.

And so, perforce we compel him to belief in the Sefirot, or he is called a heretic. And by this path it is necessitated that one who says he has no dealing with Kabbalah, and does not wish to direct his prayer except to the Master of the lights — as many have thought — surely is called one who errs. For if a person comes to speak of the simple One in respect of its aspect toward its [own] existence, apart from its existence and its aspect in respect of the Sefirot, he is found to remove its actions altogether. For the Ein Sof, in respect of the aspect of its essence, is simple and is not a possessor of changes — that it should change from judgment to mercy, and be moved by will, and change from will to will through prayer — except in respect of its aspect toward its Sefirot, which are its [acts of] providence, and through which the change of judgment and mercy occurs. And let the inquirer not press to enter, by means of these our words, within the partition, to understand the matter of the changes and the providence — for harm will reach him, and not benefit; rather, we shall explain the matter at length in the Gate of Essence and Vessels, with God's help. In sum: a person is compelled to believe in the Sefirot in order to be correct in the cardinal principles of the faith and in its corners, which cannot be upheld except through them — that is, by means of them — for through them the Emanator effects the changes, and from this no change whatsoever reaches Him, God forbid, as is explained at length in that lovely Gate. And of God we ask forgiveness.

After we have occupied ourselves with the matter of the Sefirot, and the necessity of their existence, and the matter transmitted concerning them among the sages, we need to know their essence and their names — the comprehensive [naming] agreed upon among the commentators, and in particular in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him. And this is it: the first, Keter; the second, Chokhmah; the third, Binah; the fourth, Gedulah or Chesed; the fifth, Pachad or Gevurah; the sixth, Tiferet; the seventh, Netzach; the eighth, Hod; the ninth, Yesod; the tenth, Malkhut. And these Sefirot are ten Names that may not be erased; and the Names and the Sefirot are all one thing, for the spirituality of the Names is the very Sefirot. Keter is Ehyeh, and it is not found in Scripture except three times in one verse (Exodus 3:14): "And God said to Moses, Ehyeh asher Ehyeh (I will be what I will be); and He said, Thus shall you say to the children of Israel, Ehyeh has sent me to you." But the reason it does not appear [more] in the Torah, and other doubts in this inquiry, will be explained in the Gate of Names, with the help of God. And the Name of Chokhmah is Yah, and there are many of these written: in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "My strength and song is Yah," and "For a hand is upon the throne of Yah." Repeated in the Prophets: "I shall not see Yah, Yah, in the land of the living," which is in the writing of Hezekiah. Tripled in the Writings: "From the straits I called Yah; Yah answered me with expansiveness," and many like them. And the Name of Binah is the four-letter Name with the vocalization of Elohim, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "Adonai YHVH, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it," and many like it. Repeated in the Prophets: "YHVH Adonai is my strength, and He makes my feet [like hinds']," etc., and many like it. Tripled in the Writings: "I will come in the mighty acts of Adonai YHVH; I will make mention of Your righteousness, Yours alone," and many like it. And the Name of Chesed is the Name El, and there are many of these in the Torah, in the Prophets, and in the Writings. In the Torah: "And he called it El, God of Israel," and many like it. In the Prophets: "El, Elohim, YHVH — He knows," etc., and many like it. In the Writings: "El, whose way is perfect," and many like it. And the Name of Gevurah is Elohim, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And Elohim tested Abraham," and many like it. Repeated in the Prophets: "And there was a terror of Elohim," and many like it. Tripled in the Writings: "Arise, O Elohim, judge the earth," and many like it. And the Name of Tiferet is YHVH — written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And YHVH said," "And YHVH spoke," and many others. Repeated in the Prophets: "Thus said YHVH," and many others. Tripled in the Writings: "YHVH said to me, You are My son," and many like it. And the Name of Netzach you will not find alone, but only joined with the Name of Hod — for the reason that the two of them have one Name, which is Tzeva'ot. And this is not found in the Torah at all; but in the Prophets, many: "Thus said YHVH Tzeva'ot," and many others. And as for the Name of Yesod, all the later commentators explained that its proper Name is El Chai. But this is difficult, for El Chai is not among the Names that may not be erased — for the word Chai is not holy, as it appears in Tractate Shevuot (35a), where they counted there only [the Name] El. And the Name El, which is the holy one, is borrowed for it from Chesed by way of the epithets, and they counted it. And among those holding this view is Rabbi Abba in the book of the Zohar, Parashat Vayikra (11a), and these are his words: "The sixth and the seventh are called Tzeva'ot. The eighth is El Chai, as it is said, 'For there YHVH commanded the blessing — life,' etc.; and this is the Tzaddik, from whom all life issues."

And as for his having counted Netzach and Hod as sixth and seventh — although they are seventh and eighth, as is known — it is because Rabbi Abba began to count the Names from the Name Yah, from Chokhmah, as is explained there. And he explained that the Tzaddik is called El Chai for the reason that the issuing-place of life is from him; and he said "from whom all life issues," because the root of life is above, in Chokhmah and Binah, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "wisdom gives life to its possessors," and as we shall explain in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions, with the help of God. For this [reason] he said that the reason Yesod is called by the Name El Chai — although the root of life is above — is because he is their source in respect of their issuing forth; and on that account he adopted the expression "issue" (nafkin), that is, in respect of issuing.

Behold, then, that Rabbi Abba explained that the Name of Yesod is El Chai. And Rabbi Elazar (there, 11b) disputed him and said that its Name is Shaddai, and these are his words: "The ninth is Shaddai, for He said to the world, 'Enough (dai)' — for 'dai' is sufficiency; and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world (yesod olam), who said to the world, 'Enough.'"

And because it was difficult for Rabbi Elazar that the Name Shaddai means "He said to the world, Enough" — that is, that He set it a limit, in that its boundaries were stretching ever onward until He said to it, "Enough" — and this cannot rightly apply to Yesod, since the creation of the world was by way of the Architect, which is Malkhut, and so it is surely she who said to the world, "Enough" — therefore he said that Shaddai means sufficiency and sustenance, and the sustenance is from the side of Yesod, and it is he who supplies sustenance to the world; and this is "and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world." And he intended to say [the acrostic] Tzaddik-Yesod-Olam, for he is the foundation that establishes the world; and this is why he doubled his expression and said, "the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world, who said to the world, 'Enough.'" Even so, we do not deny that the Name El Chai is in Yesod, as Rabbi Abba explained — but not that it is a holy Name in the manner of the other Names that may not be erased, but rather an epithet like the other epithets; and it comes in Scripture (Psalms 84:3): "my heart and my flesh sing out to El, the living God (El Chai)." And the Name Shaddai is written in the Torah: "And El Shaddai will bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you"; repeated in the Prophets: "like the voice of Shaddai when they went"; tripled in the Writings: "and Shaddai will be your defense." And the Name of Malkhut is Adonai, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And now, let the power of Adonai be magnified," and many like it; repeated in the Prophets: "A word has the Adonai sent against Jacob," and many like it; tripled in the Writings: "Adonai, open my lips," and many like it. And it has come in the Masorah that there are 134 of them in Scripture; and the reason for this you will find in Chizkuni's commentary on the Torah, at its beginning, where he said that this number corresponds to the letters of the initial and final letters of the words mizrach (east), ma'arav (west), darom (south) — to say that these three directions are shut up in the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He; and likewise [the number] 134 (k-l-d) is a term of shutting, like aklidei (keys); but north is not included, for it is open, to exact [punishment] from the wicked, and in the time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will shut it up as well, etc. — see there, and you will find reasons that follow from this inquiry. And these ten aforementioned Names are palaces (heikhalot) for the spirituality of the Sefirot; and that spirituality is a garment for their inner spirituality, alluded to in the four-letter Name within each and every Sefirah. And this matter, and others besides it, in the explanation of these Names and the matters of the Sefirot, will be explained in the coming Gates, with the help of God, each and every one in its fitting place.
And so this Gate is concluded; and thanks be to God, who has helped us — may He help us — forever, Selah, and ever. Amen.
The Second Gate is the Gate of the Reason for the Emanation:

On the reason why ten, and not more. And after we occupied ourselves in the preceding Gate with the necessity of the matter of the Emanation — and [established] that it is agreed among the Kabbalists that they are ten, no fewer and no more — and arranged their matter and their names, we have seen fit, in this Gate, to give a reason for their being ten, and [to address] the matter of the Emanation as a whole, in general, with the help of God.
Chapter One:

As we were taking delight in the Edenic gardens of the books of the sages in this wisdom, we found that the sage Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, in his book Minchat Yehudah (folio 9b), wrote, concerning the reason for the ten, one reason in the name of Rabbi Azriel, with its refutation alongside it. And these are his words: "Know that every point comes with three diameters — length, breadth, and depth — and when you multiply these one by another by way of number, the square of the three makes nine; and together with the place that bears them, they are ten" — thus far Rabbi Azriel, of blessed memory. And Rabbi Yehudah objected to him, and these are his words: "And this reason does not seem good to me, for two reasons. The first: that the premise is not true, because the aforementioned diameters are possessors of quantity, whereas the point has no quantity, for it is the end of the line. And further: would it seem good in the eyes of YHVH that the aforementioned diameters, by which body is defined, should be attributed to the Emanation — when, in divinity, body has vanished and gone its way?"

And because his words are somewhat closed — in particular in the first objection, in his saying "the point has no quantity," etc. — we have seen fit to explain his intent. The matter is this: every corporeal thing has length and breadth and depth, and there is no corporeal thing in the world that does not have these three, for they are the defining properties of body. And were one to conceive two defining properties of body alone — namely length and breadth, without depth — it is called a plane (shetach), whose meaning is like a color spread upon the face of the paper, to which length and breadth rightly apply but depth does not, and which is therefore called a plane. And when we conceive a single defining property of body alone — namely length, but not breadth — it is called a line (kav): that is, the line of length, stripped of breadth, and all the more of depth. And when we conceive the negation of the three defining properties of body, that matter is called a point (nekudah): the matter that has neither length nor breadth nor depth — not because it can be in reality, but it is called a notional point (nekudah tzurit), that is, a depiction of the negation of the defining properties of body, and not that it should be in reality. And with this premise the intent of Rabbi Yehudah will be understood, who objected to Rabbi Azriel that his words are self-contradictory, in that he said "a point comes with three diameters" — and this is impossible, for a point has neither length nor breadth nor depth, but is the end of the line; that is, as we explained, that it is the end of the line, which is also itself a negation of length, and the point is thus found to be without any diameters at all. And his saying that it is the end of the line is not agreed upon among the masters of the [mathematical] science. For some say that two points, or more, gathered together make a line; and some say that even if all the points in the world were gathered, they would not make the line, since the point has no length at all, [and so] it is impossible that length should come to be through it. But this is not of the essence of our occupation.

Now Rabbi Yehudah, with respect to his two objections against the view of Rabbi Azriel, answered by way of number, to vindicate Rabbi Azriel; and because the matter is not seemly and acceptable, we have not copied it here. And it seems to us [right] to argue the reverse, in vindication of Rabbi Azriel, and we say: it is true that the Emanation is not body and not corporeality; even so, from it body and corporeality proceed. And just as the masters of Kabbalah believed that there are four elements — namely water, fire, air, earth — alluded to in the Sefirot, these being Gedulah the element of water, Gevurah the element of fire, Tiferet the element of air, and Malkhut the element of earth — yet not that they are literally elements, God forbid, but rather that they are the root of the elements, and the elements are created from their root — so it is in the matter of the defining properties of body: the matter is not that there is literally body above, nor that the defining properties of body rightly apply to the Sefirot; rather, since body is created from them, and they are its root, there is found in the roots, by way of epithet, the existence of the defining properties of body. And therefore it can rightly be said, above, "length, breadth, and depth" — the intent being the power by which length is made, the power by which breadth is made, and the power by which depth is made. And likewise each one of these three powers performs three other actions, so that their existence is found to be nine. And the one who brings about the existence of body, prior to its coming to its defining properties, is a tenth power. Thus we are compelled [to posit] above ten powers, which are ten Sefirot. And not that the view of Rabbi Azriel is that there are above the defining properties of body, God forbid. Furthermore, it appears that from the outset the objection has no force at all, for Rabbi Azriel did well in likening the Emanation to the defining properties of body — for license has already been given for this matter.

And so, in Sefer Yetzirah, [the author] took this very path, in saying: depth of above and depth of below, and above and below, and east and west, and south and north — these are the defining properties of body; yet even so, [the author of] Sefer Yetzirah did not restrain himself from likening it to divinity, since they are a parable and a likeness in the inquiry. And as for the second objection — that the point has no quantity — this is no objection. For there is surely no point that is not a possessor of the [defining] properties; and if we said above that the point has no quantity, that is specifically the notional point, which is not in reality, whereas the point that is in reality is a possessor of diameters — and so this is no objection.
And further, since the Emanation is not body and corporeality, he called it by the term "point," which is not a body — since the Emanation is the root of body and of its defining properties.

And further, he called the Emanation by the term "point" to say that, just as the point is unified in its parts and does not admit of parts at all, so the Emanation does not admit of parts; and even if we speak of parts in it, all is parable and likeness. Thus far has reached what has seemed to us [in arguing] the reverse, in vindication of Rabbi Azriel. And now let us write what Rabbi Yehudah wrote concerning the reason for the Emanation, and these are his words: "Since the Emanation comes by way of a point, we must perforce admit that there is in this point a beginning, a middle, and an end. We must admit an end, since we see that, had they been created from the side of the power that has no end, they would have gone on without end and would have existed forever — and this was not the intent; and since it has an end, then it has a beginning, for there is no end without a beginning, and no beginning without an end. And beware of thinking, by my saying 'beginning, middle, and end,' that the intent is a beginning, middle, and end in quantity, God forbid; rather, [it is] in the matter of power, for there is a difference between the cause and the effect. And because all three aforementioned termini in the point are each composed of the three — for in the beginning there is end and middle, and likewise in the middle, and likewise in the end — they are found to rise to nine, when we multiply three by three by way of the square number, and the place that bears [them], etc." — thus far his words.

These are some of his words, in brief; and he brought many passages from the Zohar as proof. And because the passages are no proof at all for his words, we have not seen fit to copy them. And what is fitting to raise as a difficulty — whether against his words or against the words of Rabbi Azriel, peace be upon him — is this: since the reason for the ten is the point, which is a possessor of three, and each composed of three, then let us also say that each part of the three that is in each of the three parts is composed of the three, and they will rise without end, from three to three. And if we do not wish to compound them in this manner, then whence comes to us the first compounding that we make, of three into nine? And this is surely a great strain. So that, on account of this, there are those who wished to combine two views together, and said that every point has depth and length and breadth, and each one of these three has beginning, middle, and end — thus nine — and the place that bears [them], thus ten. And it is in my power to object against the holders of these three views, for I see no place for these matters — since [on their account] bodies and limit are found to be a necessity for the existence of the Emanation. And this is an unacceptable thing — that we should say that, because these are necessary defining properties, the Sefirot were compelled to have their measure thus; for the Sefirot acted and gave birth to the world and all the creatures. And behold, if the Sefirot were sixteen, it would be possible for there to be, in the reality of the defining properties, sixteen things, four by four. And who has seen [fit] to necessitate the bringing-about of the form of the father on account of the existence of the form of the son? Would you say that Reuben was compelled to have hands so that his son should have hands — or, likewise, that Reuben [should have] three hands so that his son should have three hands? And how can we necessitate the form of the cause on account of the form of the effect? For in truth the cause is the principal, and the effect is subordinate to it; and how can the effect be a necessity for the form of the existence of its cause? I am astonished.

And further, regarding the words of Rabbi Yehudah, who said that the point has beginning, middle, and end, and that each of the three should have beginning, middle, and end — this too does not work out well. For the middle cannot possibly have an end and a beginning; for if it had an end and a beginning, it would not be a middle, and what is a middle cannot rightly have an end and a beginning, since its beginning is the first beginning and its end is the last end. For "end" and "beginning" are not a quantitative end and beginning, but [rather] the cessation of power or its beginning. And how is it possible to say that there is a power that would be the cessation of its [own] power, or its beginning — unless [it be] its last cessation or its first beginning, that is, its own beginning and its own end?

And further, since the intent in "beginning" and "end" is only the matter of the cessation of power or its beginning, as has been explained — then, since the end is the cessation of power, how can we, in that cessation, say [that there is] a beginning and a middle, for it is nothing but a cessation, since the power has ceased, and in a cessation there is no beginning and middle? — though it is possible to settle some of this with difficulty. And concerning that which he objected against Rabbi Azriel — that the diameters of the corporeal, how can they be attributed to the Emanation, since in divinity, etc. — for him too, is it [any] easier? How can the cessation of power and the beginning of power fall within the Emanation, since in divinity no deficiency of power can rightly be [posited], God forbid, for it is whole, the utmost of perfection? And perforce we must answer to this one of two things. The first: that it was necessitated for the reason that there is a difference between the Ein Sof and the emanated, like the difference between cause and effect; and therefore some cessation of power can rightly be [posited] of it, since of necessity it is not exactly like the Emanator, for the reason that it descended from Him and is emanated from Him; and this matter is no deficiency in the Emanator, God forbid, nor in the emanated, but [is] only because it is emanated and an effect, and [so] it was compelled to descend a degree from the cause; and this is on account of the superiority of the Emanator over the emanated, and for this reason some cessation of power can rightly be [posited] of it. Or [secondly], we may say that a limit was necessitated in their action, in order to fulfill the intent of the Emanator, which was that the creatures should be possessors of an end and possessors of cessation. If so, then according to the words of Rabbi Azriel too we may say that limit was necessitated in the Emanation for these reasons. First: because the First Cause is the utmost negation of cessation, and of depiction, and of quantity altogether; yet the [beings] emanated from it were compelled, according to their descent from before His face, to be limited somewhat by a notional limit, and not a literal limit — yet in respect of the Emanator, who is their cause, from whom we are obligated to negate limit and cessation and the other matters resembling these, it was necessitated that the emanated have a difference from Him, like the difference of the effect from the cause.

And further, second: in order that the creatures that proceed from the emanated be possessors of limit — and this is His power, blessed be He: for just as the world was created something from nothing (yesh me-ayin), so the Ein Sof, King of kings of kings, emanated emanated [beings], from which would proceed actions that are possessors of an end, in order that the creatures be possessors of limit. And the one who inquires into this must understand his [Rabbi Azriel's] view, and establish it, and support it, and set it straight toward the truth. And let him not think that our intent in this is to set a limit, either in the Emanator or in the emanated, God forbid and Heaven forbid. Rather, the intent in this is that, after we negate body and limit and quantity and the cessation of power and the end and the terminus from the pure and holy Emanation — the utmost of negation and removal — we are then compelled, of absolute necessity, to ascend yet [another] degree, higher and more select, to the Ein Sof, the Emanator, King of kings of kings. And therefore they called Him Ein Sof (Without End), for the reason mentioned. And paucity of speech in this matter is good and seemly; and of this, and the like, it is said (Proverbs 27:26), "lambs are for your clothing." Even so, we have seen fit to necessitate the matter from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 70, folio 130a), and these are his words: "The supernal Keter, although it is the primordial light, a clear light, a refined light — it is dark before the Cause of Causes."

The intent is: although it is a clear light, etc. — the utmost of purity, and it is without limit, and we are obligated to negate from it density and limit — even so, we are obligated to believe that it has density and limit and a cessation of light and power in respect of the Emanator, who is its cause. And for this [reason] he used this expression for the Ein Sof, the expression "the Cause of Causes"; and the intent is to necessitate the matter of absolute necessity, for He is the Cause of all the causes, and therefore He is necessarily superior to them all. For were we to negate from the Emanation every deficiency in the world, and to elevate it to the most perfect degree possible in the world, there would follow from this the denial of the existence of a First Cause — since, [if] Keter is at a degree above which there is no degree, then what is the degree by which the Emanator would be elevated above it? Therefore we are obligated to give a place by which we may elevate the Emanator above all the emanated, even as we elevate the emanated in every [way] possible. And this matter a person must contemplate; and let him not be alarmed into replying quickly.

Rabbi Yehudah wrote yet another reason, and wrote that it is more sufficient than the reason of Rabbi Azriel that we copied in the preceding chapter, and these are his words: "The comprehensive number is ten; there is none besides it. And this is so because everything that is above ten returns to the units — whether from the side of the units, like 11, 12, 13, or from the side of the tens, like 20, 30, 40, which are the doubling of the array of the tens. And since the Emanation enters into number, it is fitting that it take hold of the most comprehensive among the numbers" — thus far his words.

And as for what he said, "since the Emanation enters into number" — the meaning is that they were compelled to be possessors of number, so that the creatures should be possessors of number and limit, as we explained above. And what may be raised as a difficulty is this: what causes the comprehensive number to be ten, and not twenty, and not a hundred — and [why is it] that [only] from twenty and upward is there a return of the steps? We answer that the cause of this was the Sefirot's being ten; for if the Sefirot were twenty, the number too would rise to twenty. And this is surely true; and this is a more sufficient and more acceptable reason — that the Sefirot are the principal and the number subordinate, and not the reverse, that the number should be ten without reason; and this [the Sefirot] would be the cause of the Emanation in its number.

And further: the Sefirot are a cause preceding all the creatures, and they are causes to all that is from them and below; and if so, how can the number, which is the later, be a cause to the Sefirot, which precede? And this is surely a great strain. And although we reject these answers as a reason for the Emanation, we do not deny that there is truth [in them]: for number and the Emanation have a relation and a great connection — for the matter of number is ten, and it rises from ten to ten without end, and never rises beyond ten; so it is in the matter of the Sefirot.

And further: the numbers are ten, and from ten they rise to a hundred, and from a hundred they rise to a thousand — and this is "thousand" (elef), which is one (echad), in the secret of the return of the matter to perfect unity, like the matter of the Sefirot, [which return] in all of them. For ten times ten is a hundred; further, when we compound them once more, they are a thousand — that is, alef, in the secret of pele (wonder), which is the return of things to their source, in the secret of the unity. And likewise, further, there are several great cardinal principles that depend upon number, which are cardinal principles of the Torah, as we shall write in the Gate of Combination, with the help of God. And let us not think that there is anything in the world more resembling the Emanation than the matter of number. And likewise, too, we do not deny that it is true that the Emanation is three of three [each] three, and a comprehensive power — that is, three, which are Chesed, Din, and Rachamim, and in each one of them three: namely, in Chesed, beginning-middle-end — that is, Chokhmah the beginning, Chesed the middle, and Netzach the end; and likewise in Din, the beginning is Binah, the middle Gevurah, and the end Hod; and likewise in Rachamim, Tiferet the beginning, Yesod the middle, and Malkhut the end; and the supernal Keter comprehends them all — as we shall expand this explanation in the Gate of Essence and Governance, ch.25, with God's help. And this matter is deep, as we shall expound at length there. But even so, let us believe in truth what is true: that these matters are no sufficient reason for the Emanation at all, as explained above. Rabbi Menachem Recanati, of blessed memory, wrote yet another reason for the seven Sefirot of construction, one by one, in his book on the Reasons of the Commandments which is his, in the matter of the inquiry into the essences and the vessels; and Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, of blessed memory, copied his language. [Recanati:] "And now we shall explain how the world needs these seven extremities, which are Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malkhut. The beginning of the construction is Chesed, for there can be no construction without this — that is, that by this attribute the Holy One, blessed be He, whitens the iniquities of Israel; and in Sefer Yetzirah He called this attribute 'the whitener of the iniquities of Israel,' who pardons them for what is done from the side of Gevurah, since the evil inclination is emanated from there. And this Sefirah is emanated from Binah, which is above it. But the first three are intellective, and are not called attributes, and we are not now [engaged] in their explanation. And this is the great lovingkindness that the Holy One, blessed be He, does with His creatures: that He passes over [sin], first by first, and is appeased toward them, even though the [strict] law does not so warrant; and therefore the world cannot endure without this pillar. And in Sefer ha-Bahir I found thus: the attribute of Chesed said, 'All the days that Abraham was in the world, I had no need to do my work, for Abraham stood there in my place and kept my watch; for this is my work, that I make the world meritorious, even if they have been [found] liable.'"

"'And further, I bring them back and put into their hearts to do the will of their Father in Heaven' — all this Abraham did. Further, the world needs the second pillar, which is Din (Judgment), and it is the opposite of the first attribute we mentioned; and were it not for this pillar, punishment would not reach the wicked, and every man would rob and kill his fellow with none exacting [it] from him; therefore the world needs to be conducted by this pillar, in order to exact [punishment] from the wicked. And this Sefirah is emanated from the Chesed we mentioned, and is called 'fire from water' — that is, fire that issued from water; and just as water is the opposite of fire, so the actions of this attribute are the opposite of the action of the other attribute. And these two are called 'the arms of the world,' as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:27), 'and underneath are the everlasting arms.' Further, the world needs a third pillar, which is Tiferet, and it is the intermediate attribute, and receives from both, and stands between the two. And the need that the world has for this attribute is because, by the first two attributes, there is not enough for the world: for one who became liable, were he judged by the second attribute — which is the attribute of judgment — would be judged without compassion, as is the attribute of harsh judgment; and it would also [punish] the meritorious and the wholly good above. And were he judged by the attribute of Chesed, his few iniquities would not be recalled to him, even in this world. Therefore the world needs the intermediate attribute, like a person who joins two things as one and unites them in a single subject, in order to give to each man according to his way and according to the fruit of his deeds — that if the righteous have sinned, [punishment] is exacted from them in this world, and if the wicked have performed commandments, their good reward is paid them in this world. And this attribute is called 'east' (mizrach), for from there light went forth to the world; and the sphere of the sun is set against it, for the measure of the day is emanated from it. Further, the world needs a fourth pillar and a fifth pillar, which are Netzach and Hod, which are emanated and flow from the Gedulah and the Gevurah that we mentioned above, as it is said (Psalms 16:11), 'pleasantness in Your right hand, Netzach' — that is, that Netzach is on the right, aligned beneath Chesed, and Hod on the left, aligned beneath Gevurah."

"And the matter of Netzach is from the matter of 'prevailing' (nitzuach) — that is, that by that attribute, the Chesed and the merit prevail over the accusers. And therefore one must give thanks to YHVH; and this is Hod, from the language of 'acknowledgment' (hoda'ah) to the Name, who founded this pillar — for were it not for the help of YHVH to a person, he could not stand before the Satan. Further, the world needs a sixth pillar and a seventh pillar, which are Yesod and Malkhut, and they are the likeness of male and female; and all is emanated to Malkhut, called the Shekhinah and the Assembly of Israel (Knesset Yisrael), in which all the Sefirot dwell, as we already explained above. And therefore our Sages of blessed memory called her 'bride' (kallah), and in the Song of Songs too she is called 'bride,' because she is composed (kelulah) of all; and she is in the west (ma'arav), as our Sages of blessed memory said, 'the Shekhinah is in the west,' because there all is mingled (mit'arev)." — thus far [Recanati's] explanation of the reason for the Emanation. And although it is true that most of his words are correct, even so these matters are not sufficient for the reason of the Emanation. For since judgment and punishment, and lovingkindness and reward, are in the two attributes Chesed and Gevurah, and the intermediate attribute is Tiferet — what further need is there for the rest of the Sefirot? For why should the vanquishing of the accuser and the evil inclination not be in Gevurah, as it in truth is — and so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained, that a person's prevailing over his inclination is from the side of Gevurah; and we shall expand on this in the Gate of Essence and Governance, ch.3. And likewise, acknowledgment is not an active attribute, according to his words, but [merely] that a person should give thanks to the Name; and was it for [the sake of] giving thanks to YHVH — which a person must [do] — that it was necessary to emanate one Sefirah? I am astonished. Further, Yesod and Malkhut — to what end? For since Chesed and Din come into mediation and are unified, what need is there for male and female at all, for mingling — since the powers were already mingled in the mediation?
And further, that we cannot give a reason in this manner for the first three at all, as he himself said in his explanation.

And further — God forbid — was the hand of the Emanator truly too short to emanate one single emanation alone, that is, a single Sefirah in which there would be the power of punishment and reward and mediation? And there is no answer from the language of the Mishnah (Avot 5:1), "By ten utterances the world was created — and could it not have been created by a single utterance?" etc. For on the contrary, the intent of the Mishnah is the opposite of what he said: that although the creation of the world was by differing matters indicating judgment and mercy and mediation, even so it would have been possible for its creation to be by the power of a single utterance — that is, a single Sefirah — as it appears that it was not beyond His power for the power of all ten to be in the power of a single Sefirah. And this is the intent of "and could it not have been created by a single utterance," etc. — surely it speaks of the creation of the world as it is now. And their saying "but [it was so] in order to exact [punishment]" — the intent is not as Rabbi Menachem imagined; rather, the intent concerns the [final] end — whether [it is] possessed of an end, or without an end, or otherwise — as we shall expand in the explanation in the coming chapters, with the help of God. And therefore this reason does not fulfill our desire, nor quench our thirst, at all.

After we have written, in the preceding chapters, all the reasons that the commentators wrote — be they many or few — and roused [objections] against them according to what they have shown us from Heaven, we have resolved to speak on this matter according to what falls to our lot. And first of all let us say: "In men I have seen [worth]; a [decisive] refutation I have not seen." For this question cannot escape being one of two ways. Either the question of the reason for the ten is [directed] to us — that is, whence have we proof, from the Torah or from inquiry, for our received tradition; or this question is [directed] to the Emanator, the Ein Sof, King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He: why did He emanate ten, and not some other number? And to each of these we shall reply. If the question is to us — that is, whence have we support for the tradition that they are ten, that we should [not rather] say they are twenty, or five, or one — then from the outset it is no question, for we have proof upon proof in the Torah of Moses, which reveals to us and illumines our eyes in these hidden secrets: whether in the creation of the world by ten utterances; or in the giving of the Torah by ten Commandments; and David, king of Israel, peace be upon him, [attested it] by the ten kinds of praise in the psalm "Praise El in His sanctuary," with which he sealed his book. And this matter has already been explained in Tractate Rosh Hashanah (32a), where we learn there: "These ten Kingships — corresponding to what? Rebbi said: corresponding to the ten praises that David said in the book of Psalms. — There are many praises! — Those in which it is written, 'Praise Him with the blast of the shofar.' Rav Yosef said: corresponding to the Ten Commandments that were spoken to Moses at Sinai. Rabbi Yochanan said: corresponding to the ten utterances by which the world was created. — Which are they? 'And [God] said,' 'And [God] said,' in [the account of] Genesis. — There are [only] nine! — 'In the beginning' (Bereshit) is also an utterance, as it is written, 'By the word of YHVH the heavens were made.'"
The truth is that this passage is, on its face, difficult in the matter of Rabbi Yochanan, who answered, "In the beginning is also an utterance."

Now, [the word "In the beginning"] alludes to Chokhmah, which is called "beginning" (reshit), and the large bet [of Bereshit] alludes to it. If so, then even though "In the beginning" is also an utterance, there are still [only] nine — and this is difficult: for then what was difficult to the questioner? If he objected that Chokhmah is not in the count, then there would be eight, and he should have objected [accordingly]. And if he objected that Keter is not in the count, then why was it resolved when he answered "In the beginning," etc.? — for he should have objected: although "In the beginning" is also an utterance, even so, with "In the beginning" there are still [only] nine, since "In the beginning" is Chokhmah. This is a general question concerning the utterances mentioned in this passage. And likewise, from this difficulty we may establish the view of Rabbi Shem Tov ben Shem Tov, author of Sefer ha-Emunot, whose language we shall copy in the Gate [of] "Whether the Ein Sof is the Keter," ch.3 — and it is the view of [those who hold] Da'at, who hold that Keter is not in the count of the Sefirot, but the ten Sefirot are from Chokhmah and below; and because the count pressed him, he said that another Sefirah was introduced for him, called Da'at, and it is below Chokhmah and Binah and above Chesed and Gevurah. And we shall expand on the matter there. Now, according to his words, it is found that the utterances begin only from Chokhmah; and even so there are nine without "In the beginning," which is Chokhmah, and ten with "In the beginning," which is Chokhmah. And because of the ruin that follows from this passage — before we rouse further objections against it and explain a general principle in it — it is fitting that we look into the rectification of this matter, and we say that this matter is impossible. For since Rabbi Shem Tov admitted with his [own] mouth that Da'at is the one mentioned in the verse (Proverbs 3:20), "by His knowledge (da'ato) the depths were cleaved," and likewise from what our Sages of blessed memory said (Chagigah 12a — and there it is: "by ten things the world was created," the third of them being Chokhmah, etc.), "by three things the world was created: by Chokhmah, by Tevunah, and by Da'at" — it is necessitated from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that Da'at is the [hidden] existence of Tiferet, concealed between Abba and Imma; and this is what is called BeN-YaH, by which the union of Chokhmah and Binah [occurs], as we shall expand on these matters in that Gate.

Now, according to this, it is fitting that we ask: how does this Da'at — which is the existence of the concealed Tiferet, emanated between Abba and Imma — differ [so as] to perform an utterance in its own right, from the rest of the existences of the Sefirot, which did not perform utterances, even though their coming-into-being already preceded the coming-into-being of this Da'at? — such as the existence of Binah concealed in Chokhmah: for just as Chokhmah itself acted, it would be fitting that the concealed Binah also act; and likewise the existence of Gevurah concealed in Binah, and the existence of Chesed concealed in Chokhmah — it would have been fitting that each of them perform one utterance, apart from the utterance that it has in its revealed existence, in the manner of Da'at and Tiferet. And one cannot say that the reason Da'at performed an utterance in its own right was because Da'at is the existence of Tiferet when its consort is at its side — and they are the existence of the two great luminaries — and because they were united, the two of them together performed one utterance, like the rest of the Sefirot; but after the moon brought accusation and was diminished and banished, the luminaries were divided into two, and Tiferet again performed an utterance in its own right and Malkhut an utterance in its own right. For if so, why did Tiferet not, from the outset, perform an utterance for itself and Malkhut for itself, even though they were united in the utmost union? For one cannot deny that they were two Sefirot; for if not — if they are reckoned as only one Sefirah — then the Sefirot are found, before the diminishment, to be nine and not ten, since Malkhut and Tiferet are one Sefirah; and likewise, when [the moon] returns to its original place, there will be nine — and this is precluded by the law of this wisdom, as explained in the preceding Gate.

And further: the ten Commandments and the ten utterances are one matter, as is proved from the passage we copied above, and as is likewise proved in the Zohar, Parashat Yitro (93b), and these are its words: "These ten utterances of the Torah are the sum of all the commandments of the Torah, the sum of upper and lower, the sum of all the ten utterances of Creation."

And [the Zohar] said "the sum of all the commandments of the Torah," because Rashbi, peace be upon him, holds thus: that the 613 commandments are included in the ten Commandments, as is explained in Parashat Yitro, and are likewise included in the ten utterances, as is proved in Parashat Bereshit and in the Tikkunim. And therefore [the Zohar] said that the ten Commandments are the sum of the commandments. And likewise it said that they are the sum of the ten utterances — meaning that all that is expounded from the ten utterances of the account of Creation is expounded from the ten Commandments at the giving of the Torah, in the eyes of the enlightened. Now let us say: since the ten Commandments and the ten utterances are all one, then how is it possible to say of the Commandments that [the Sefirot] were united and the Shekhinah was banished? For surely, after she was united in the coupling, she was not diminished while she was in the bosom of her spouse; and if she were below, why are they ten — for Da'at was already concealed, and it would not have been fitting that an utterance be said [by it], since it was already concealed and the matter had not returned to its rectification.

And further, can we say that, had there been no diminishment, the utterances would have been only nine? I am astonished — for [then] the world would have lacked, of its perfection, all the matters of that one utterance.

And further, since Da'at comprehends Malkhut and Tiferet, then [as for] the utterance by which it said that that creation was created — why did it not create all that was possible by the power of Malkhut and all that was possible by the power of Tiferet, since it is the existence of their union, namely their being two great luminaries? And why did there yet remain a creation [to be done] by Malkhut and Tiferet afterward? Was the power of Da'at — which is more complete than the two of them — deficient?

And further, we have several clear proofs that "In the beginning" is the utterance of the supernal Keter. First, in Sefer ha-Bahir, of blessed memory: "What are the utterances? The first — the supernal Keter, blessed and praised, etc.; Chokhmah is the second, as it is written, etc." — thus it counted the supernal Keter among the utterances, and it is the first of them all.

And further, the difficulty is, from the outset, no difficulty and no necessity — because, although the word "In the beginning" (Bereshit) is in Chokhmah, even so the utterance is in Keter; and on account of the fineness of Keter and its nearness to its source — such that nothing of the four-letter Name is attributed to it except the thorn of the yod, and it is likewise called alef, from the language of pele (wonder), and is called "a hidden and concealed Amon" — even though the bet of Bereshit is the allusion to Chokhmah, all the same its thorn indicates Keter. And so Rabbi Akiva explained, and these are his words: "They say to the bet: who created you? — and it shows, by its thorn, toward the alef." And the intent is that the bet itself, which is Chokhmah among the existents — which is not the first to the Emanation, but is the second emanation — has a thorn behind it, to point toward the alef, as though pointing, for those who ask it, "who created you?" — that is, [asking] whether it was emanated by an emanated [being] or by a first Emanator; and it shows, by its thorn, that it is the second emanation, and that the alef, which is Keter, preceded it. And now it can rightly be [said] that the utterance "In the beginning" is in Keter, even though the word "In the beginning" alludes to Chokhmah, since Keter is already alluded to in it somewhat, as explained. And the matter is that, in the verse "In the beginning," the whole Emanation is included, to indicate concerning it that it is the Emanator — that is, by the power of the Ein Sof — and even so, Keter itself is the Emanator and the agent who speaks the utterance. And likewise it is found that most of the utterances are composed of all ten; and therefore, in the word "In the beginning," there came an allusion to Chokhmah, even though the essence of the utterance is in Keter. And this is no wonder, for the Blessing of the Patriarchs is in Chesed, yet Chesed is not mentioned in it until "God of Abraham" — and even "God of Abraham" is in Chokhmah — and it is not mentioned in essence except in the words "the great God," apart from the [concluding] seal; so it is in the matter of the utterance "In the beginning": granted that the word "In the beginning" is in Chokhmah, even so the essence of the utterance is in Keter, and it was concealed, as is its custom; and even so it came by way of allusion in the thorn of the bet, as explained — and the intent is the Chokhmah that is in Keter.

And further, besides this, one may say that the bet itself alludes to Keter; and the support for this is that the bet of Bereshit is the alef of Avgitatz, which is the forty-two-letter Name, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Particulars of the Names, with the help of God; and Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained that the alef of Avgitatz is the allusion to Keter, and these are his words (in Tikkun 70, folio 116): "The alef of Avgitatz — it is Keter, hidden, an Amon, and concealed."

Thus he testified explicitly that the bet of Bereshit is in Keter. And close to this is the view of Ramban, of blessed memory, in Parashat Bereshit, and these are his words: "And the word Bereshit alludes to Chokhmah, which is the beginning of beginnings, as I mentioned; and therefore the Jerusalem Targum rendered it 'with wisdom' (be-chokhmeta). And the word is crowned with the crown of the bet."

And the explanation of his words is that the bet alludes to Keter, for the reason that it is a "house" (bayit) for all the Sefirot. And so it is proved from his language, in his saying "and the word Bereshit alludes to Chokhmah" — the intent being the word Bereshit, not the bet, but the word itself, as he concludes that it is "beginning" (reshit), etc.; and he did not say that it is called Bereshit, but "reshit" alone; and as he brings proof from the Targum, which rendered "be-chokhmeta" — it is not literally Chokhmah, but the bet of Bereshit is a servile [prefix] letter, for the word reshit is Chokhmah, and the bet of Bereshit is Keter; and therefore he said, "and the word is crowned with the crown of the bet."

From all this it appears that there is no necessity, from this passage, [to support] the view of Rabbi Shem Tov, of blessed memory. However, it still remains incumbent upon us to explain what is found to dispute this passage in the Zohar, Parashat Vayikra. For in this passage [from Rosh Hashanah] it said that "In the beginning" is the tenth utterance, but in Parashat Vayikra (11b) Rashbi explained that they are ten utterances apart from "In the beginning." And these are his words: Rabbi Shimon said: it is written, "Ten, ten the spoon, by the shekel of the sanctuary" (Numbers 7). "Ten, ten" — to what does it come? Rather, ten for the account of Creation and ten for the giving of the Torah: ten utterances in the account of Creation and ten utterances at the giving of the Torah. With what is it concerned? Rather, because the world was created only for the sake of the Torah — for as long as Israel occupy themselves with the Torah, the world endures, and all the time that Israel are idle from the Torah, what is written? "Were it not for My covenant day and night, I would not have set the statutes of heaven and earth" (Jeremiah 33:25). Come and see: ten utterances for the account of Creation, as we learned, "By ten utterances the world was created"; ten utterances for the giving of the Torah — these are the Ten Commandments. It is written, "I am YHVH your God," and in the account of Creation it is written, "Let there be light," and there was light — this is the faith in the Holy One, blessed be He, [who] is called "light," as it is written, "YHVH is my light and my salvation," etc. It is written, "You shall have no other gods before Me," and it is written in the account of Creation, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters," etc. "Let there be a firmament" — these are Israel, who are the portion of the Holy One, blessed be He, who cleave to that place called "heaven." And this is the secret: for once Rabbi Yeisa the Elder asked Rabbi Ila'i; he said: behold, to all the other nations the Holy One, blessed be He, gave great appointed rulers; Israel — where [are they]? He sent to him: "And God set them in the firmament of the heaven" — and well did he send [reply] to him. "In the midst of the waters" — among the words of the Torah. "And it separated between water and water" — between the Holy One, blessed be He, who is called "a well of living waters," and idolatry, which is called "broken cisterns that cannot hold water," those being bitter waters, etc., putrid, gathered. And therefore the holy Israel separate between water and water. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "You shall not take the name of YHVH your God in vain," and it is written in the account of Creation, "Let the waters be gathered from under the heaven to one place." Come and see: anyone who swears by the holy Name falsely, it is as though he separated Imma (the Mother) from her place above, and the holy crowns are not settled in their places, as it is said, "and a slanderer separates the chief (aluf)" — and there is no "chief" but the Holy One, blessed be He. And it is written, "Let the waters be gathered from under the heaven to one place" — make no separation, on account of a false oath. "To one place" — as is fitting, in the place of truth, and not in another place, for falsehood. And what is falsehood? It is that the waters go to another place that is not theirs. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it," and it is written in the account of Creation, "Let the earth sprout grass, herb." When was the holy earth made fruitful and adorned with its crowns? You must say: on the Sabbath day — for then the bride was joined to the King, to bring forth grasses and blessings to the world. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "Honor your father and your mother," and it is written in the account of Creation, "Let there be luminaries in the firmament of the heaven." With what is it concerned? Rather, these luminaries — this is "your father" and "your mother": "your father," this is the sun; "your mother," this is the moon. And there is no "sun" but the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, "for a sun and a shield is YHVH God"; and there is no "moon" but the Assembly of Israel, as it is written, "and your moon shall not be withdrawn." And therefore all is one. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "You shall not murder," and it is written in the account of Creation, "Let the waters swarm [with] a living soul." And you — do not kill a person, who is called thus, as it is written, "and the man became a living soul"; do not be like these fish, [in] that the great swallow the small. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "You shall not commit adultery," and it is written in the account of Creation, "Let the earth bring forth a living soul after its kind." From here we learn that a person should not be false with another woman who is not his mate; and therefore it is written, "Let the earth bring forth a living soul after its kind" — that a woman should bear offspring only from her own kind. And who is her kind? This is her mate. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "You shall not steal," and it is written in the account of Creation, "And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed." What I have given you and deposited with you shall be yours; but do not steal what belongs to another. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "You shall not bear false witness against your fellow," and it is written in the account of Creation, "And God said, Let us make man in our image." One who is in the likeness of the King — do not bear false [witness] against him; and one who bears false witness against his fellow, it is as though he bore [false] witness above. It is written at the giving of the Torah, "You shall not covet your fellow's wife," and it is written in the account of Creation, "It is not good for the man to be alone." Behold, your mate is set opposite you; and therefore, "you shall not covet your fellow's wife." And this is [the meaning of] ten utterances for the account of Creation and ten utterances at the giving of the Torah; and this is what is written, "Ten, ten the spoon, by the shekel of the sanctuary" — they were weighed together in a single balance. And on this account the world endures, and peace is found in it. Thus far [the Zohar's] words.

And from it, it appears explicitly that, [among] the ten utterances in the account of Creation, "In the beginning" is not an utterance at all — and this is surely a strain. And in order to understand this matter, let us first set down another passage from the Tikkunim, and by means of it this perplexity will be clarified, with the help of God.

In the Tikkunim it is implied that the action of the utterances was not by any one of the three first [Sefirot] — for the first utterance is Keter, "Let there be light"; the second utterance is Chokhmah, "Let there be a firmament"; the third utterance is Binah, "Let the waters be gathered." And these are its words (in Tikkun 42, folio 79): "'In the beginning' — there is the man of whom it is said, 'and Jacob was a wholesome man (ish tam)'; and this is the third day, for there were three craftsmen up to here. The first day, the second day, and the third day — each one brought forth its handiwork. The first day, that 'hidden and concealed Amon' — that grade called Ayin, which comprises three Sefirot: alef = Keter, yod = Chokhmah, nun = Binah, etc. — said to each one of the three days that it bring forth its handiwork: it said to the first day, 'Let there be light' — at once it brought forth its handiwork and made it; this is what is written, 'and there was light.' And they have already established that there is no coming-into-being except by way of making (asiyah). The alef of Ayin, which was hovering in the air, brought forth light; the yod brought forth the firmament; the nun of Ayin brought forth the dry land; this is what is written, 'And God said, Let the waters be gathered,' etc." Thus far [the Tikkunim's] words.

It appears from it explicitly that the agents were the craftsmen, which are the six days, and they acted by the utterance of the three first [Sefirot], which are Ayin. And among what is fitting to understand, too, in the matter of these utterances, is their being ten; and although they are ten, we know that there is no creation and action except by the six days alone — which are Gedulah the first day, Gevurah the second day, Tiferet the third day, Netzach the fourth day, Hod the fifth day, Yesod the sixth day. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained that all the account of Creation is included and made by these days, in Malkhut — Malkhut brings the things forth to light in completeness. And these are his words in Parashat Terumah (127): "'Of the cedars of Lebanon' (Song 3:9) — these are the planted trees that the Holy One, blessed be He, uprooted and transplanted to another place; and these are called the cedars of Lebanon, as it is said, 'the cedars of Lebanon that he planted.' And this palanquin was not built nor perfected except by them. Again, 'of the cedars of Lebanon' — these are the six days of Creation; each and every day arranges in this palanquin the arrangement fitting to it. The first arrangement was drawn from the side of the right — the primordial light that was hidden — and was taken from the side of the right and entered into this palanquin: one form like the appearance of this light, by means of Yesod — one — and it performed in it [its] service. Afterward this palanquin brought forth one form like the appearance of this light. And this is the secret of what is written, 'Let there be light, and there was light': since it said 'Let there be light,' why is it written 'and there was light'? The verse needed only to write 'and it was so'; what is 'and there was light'? Rather, that [first] light brought forth another light fitting to it. And this is the first day of those cedars of Lebanon. The second arrangement was drawn from the side of the left — the separation of the waters by the drawing-forth of the mighty fire — and was taken from the side of the left, and entered into that palanquin and performed in it [its] service, and separated between the waters that are on the side of the right and those waters that are on the side of the left. Afterward that palanquin brought forth one form like its own. And this is the secret of what is written, 'between the waters that are below the firmament and the waters that are above the firmament,' 'and it was so.' And this is the second day of those cedars of Lebanon. The third arrangement was drawn from the side of the left and from the side of the right — one [thing], the third day, which makes peace in the world; and from there the fruits were drawn forth. And it performed [its] service in this palanquin and brought forth kind to its kind — kind for many deeds, the kind fitting to it — and all grasses and herbs and trees in many forces. And its form remained there, and that palanquin brought forth the kind in that very form. And this is the third day, which is composed of two sides, of those cedars of Lebanon. The fourth arrangement was drawn, and the light of the sun shone to illumine this palanquin within its darkness, and it entered into it to illumine, but performed no service in it until the fifth day, when this palanquin brought forth that service of the light that had entered it on the fourth day, and that palanquin brought forth [it] in that very form of that light. And this is the fourth day, one of those cedars of Lebanon. The fifth arrangement: one drawing-forth of the swarming of the waters was drawn, and it performed service to bring forth that light of the arrangement of the fourth day, and performed service in this palanquin and brought forth kinds to its kind, those that appear in that very form. And this day served that service more than all the other days. And all hung [in suspense] until the sixth day, when this palanquin brought forth all that is hidden within it, as it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth a living soul after its kind.' And this is the fifth day, one of those cedars of Lebanon.
